items.title: Copilot is "the new OS for work," and now Office runs inside of it
items.description: Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company's vision for its new "frontier ecosystem," announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as "the new OS for work." The announcement is a striking inversion of how we've traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent's work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications. items.title: Managed NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference
items.description: Serving large language models (LLMs) efficiently requires sufficient GPU memory and careful coordination of prompt processing and token generation. GLM-5.3’s FP8 weights, for example, exceed the 640 GB of GPU memory on a single ml.p5.48xlarge instance, before accounting for KV cache and runtime overhead. Long prompts can also slow token generation when both share the same GPUs. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference now supports NVIDIA Dynamo , combining Dynamo’s distributed inference capabilities with the infrastructure management of HyperPod to address these challenges. Dynamo is an open source distributed inference framework that supports multi-node deployment, disaggregated prefill and decode, and KV-aware routing with engines such as vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM. HyperPod supports these deployments with high-performance Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking, coordinated GPU scheduling, and node health monitoring and recovery. In this post, we illustrate multi-node and disaggregated serving through a deployment example, share benchmark results, and outline best practices for optimizing inference on HyperPod. How the integration works The HyperPod Inference add-on installs the Dynamo custom resource definitions and these serving and scheduling components: HyperPod Inference Operator manages endpoint deployment through an InferenceEndpointConfig (IEC) custom resource. Its dynamoSpec section supplies the Dynamo configuration. Dynamo operator manages resources defined in a DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) , including the frontend, model workers, replica counts, and resource requirements. Grove coordinates related groups of pods, including multi-node workers, and their scaling relationships. Kubernetes AI (KAI) Scheduler places pods on GPU resources, using gang scheduling to schedule the pods required for a multi-node worker together. AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) provide the Dynamo runtime, while the add-on manages integrated component versions. To adopt a supported Dynamo release, update the add-on. Deployment architecture The following diagram shows the deployment paths, serving components, and infrastructure management for disaggregated inference on SageMaker HyperPod. The Dynamo frontend routes requests to prefill workers, which process prompts, and decode workers, which generate tokens. These separate pools allow independent scaling and tuning. Both pools load the full model weights, and KV cache transfers between them over EFA. Dynamo also supports aggregated serving, where prefill and decode run in the same worker. In either topology, workers can run on one instance or span multiple instances using tensor and pipeline parallelism. Dynamo’s KV-aware router considers reusable prefix KV cache and active worker load in both topologies. Prefix reuse can reduce prompt recomputation and improve time to first token, while load awareness helps avoid overloading workers. For more details on the Dynamo architecture, see the Dynamo Knowledge Base overview . HyperPod provides node, GPU, and EFA health monitoring and manages node replacement, while the orchestration components recreate affected workers. Deployments configured through InferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec support invocation through SageMaker endpoints. Figure 1: Deployment paths, serving components, and infrastructure management for NVIDIA Dynamo on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Two ways to configure your deployment Whether you are new to HyperPod, new to Dynamo, or both, the add-on offers two deployment paths to fit your workflow: Bring-your-own DynamoGraphDeployment (DGD) lets existing Dynamo users continue using upstream documentation, recipes, and manifests, with the Dynamo operator managing the deployment. To bring an existing DGD to HyperPod, use a supported container image and configure storage, networking, and pod placement for your cluster. InferenceEndpointConfig with dynamoSpec lets existing HyperPod Inference users deploy a new Dynamo endpoint using the same configuration format and OpenAI-compatible interface they already know. For the inference engine, you can choose vLLM, SGLang, or TensorRT-LLM, with vLLM used by default. The operator also supplies defaults for KV-aware routing and replica counts. items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.description: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. items.title: Reducing token costs and latency in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore JSON workloads
items.description: As enterprises build production agents with dozens of tools and large structured inputs, token consumption and latency become the primary blockers to a good user experience. When these agents process large JSON data, every additional tool invocation injects the full payload into the large language model (LLM) context window, causing token usage and response latency to spike. Over multi-turn conversations, this pressure compounds, driving up costs and degrading response quality. Effectively managing context-window pressure in agentic systems is key to reliability and responsiveness at scale. In this post, we share three composable strategies we used to build a production agent for Flightscape that handles 20 MB+ JSON payloads. You can apply them to reduce token costs, lower latency, and maintain full reasoning capability across extended sessions. Together, these optimizations reduced token consumption by up to 71% and cut average latency by up to 80% across our benchmark runs on a representative 23 MB payload. Solution overview Flightscape is an airline operations platform that helps airlines plan and manage their crews, flights, and operations. As part of Flightscape’s crew management capabilities, we built a Training Schedule Optimization agent that verifies crew training schedule assignments against business rules. With 40+ tools and JSON inputs in megabytes, this agent could answer complex queries across crew assignments, scheduling, and resource allocation. Although the agent delivered the required functionality, average request latencies exceeded 15 seconds across most calls. Every tool call injected its full payload into the model context, inflating token counts and costs. On larger datasets, the context window filled up before the agent could finish reasoning. The following diagram (Figure 1) details the agentic architecture and data flow: Figure 1: Agent architecture and data flow In Figure 1, the Optimizer receives a Request JSON and produces a Response JSON, which is then validated by a Business Rules Validator to generate a Validation Report JSON. All three JSON documents are ingested by an AI Agent that provides a conversational interface for users to query optimization results, understand validation errors, and explore scheduling assignments. The agent is built with LangGraph , an open source framework by LangChain, and runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails can be applied to validate and filter the agent’s conversational responses, helping facilitate responsible AI practices in production deployments. We defined a custom agent state that holds the data needed by our tools: optimization request JSON, optimization response JSON, and validation report JSON. We also added basic statistics and cache data to state for rich queries. The agent uses an Amazon Bedrock model for reasoning and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to persist chat interactions across turns, and each turn follows this flow (Figure 2): Figure 2: Agentic flow This is what the state structure looks like. The state references TOPT (Training Optimizer) request and response objects, which represent the crew scheduling inputs and optimization results: class GraphState(TypedDict): """LangGraph state that combines messages with application data.""" # Messages from conversation (managed by add_messages reducer) messages: Annotated[List[BaseMessage], add_messages] # Application-specific state - parsed domain objects request: Optional[TOPTRequest] responses: List[TOPTResponse] validation_report: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] basic_stats: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] cache_data: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] Note: This state originally held heavy payloads inline. Later sections explain how we moved large artifacts out of conversational context to reduce token usage. We implemented three strategies to reduce the token costs, latency, and memory overhead caused by passing large JSON payloads through the model context. The following diagram (Figure 3) shows how the three strategies fit into a single agent turn. Strategy 1 runs at the start and end of each turn, and Strategies 2 and 3 run each time a tool returns a result. Figure 3: Overview of the three optimization strategies in one agent turn At the start of a turn, the hydrate_state() function restores lightweight session state from AgentCore memory. When a tool returns an oversized list or dictionary, the agent stores the full result in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and passes the model a compact summary with a handle. The model can then retrieve more detail with get_result_page_tool() . At the end of the turn, the dehydrate_state() function writes heavy payloads to the S3ArtifactStore and saves only references to AgentCore memory. The following sections describe each strategy in detail. Prerequisites To implement these strategies, make sure the following are in place: An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock and a supported model. An Amazon S3 bucket for artifact storage. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory enabled for session-state persistence. A LangGraph-based agent (or equivalent graph-orchestration framework) with tool-calling support. A Python 3.12+ environment with boto3 , langchain-core , and langgraph . Optimization strategies The companion code is available in this GitHub repository . Strategy 1: Persist lightweight session state, offload heavy artifacts Our first optimization was to change how we persist session state. Initially, large payloads were being stored too close to the conversational state. We therefore moved heavy artifacts (request JSON, response JSON, validation data, and other large derived payloads) to Amazon S3. items.title: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol
items.description: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol OpenAI: We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. They're available in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol . I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models. 6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions. GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20). Here are the pelicans for GPT-6.2 Sol and for GPT-6.2 Astra . The 6.2 Astra max pelican looks like this: I have a full comparison grid here , but here's how the high/xhigh/max pelicans compare with the previous Sol and Astra releases: I also ran my most recent benchmark prompt against the two models, using "Ultra' effort levels in the Codex CLI: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's Sol and here's Astra . Neither of them did a good enough job of morphing Yonkers into a big mech, at least in comparison to Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon . This video showing the Astra and Sol animations playing out at the same time: I created that video using GPT-6.2 Astra (Ultra) in the Codex desktop app by prompting: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-astra-ultra/index.html and https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-sol-ultra/index.html are two videos of the same thing by two different models I need a video of the first 10 seconds where the top half of the video plays the first and the bottom half plays the second I need an overlaid label of "GPT-6.2 Astra" on the top half and "GPT-6.2 Sol" on the bottom half. These labels should be tastefully positioned. Make the video square and 2000x2000 pixels Then later: OK make it 20s Here's the exported transcript . The buzz around these new models is mixed at the moment. Astra 6.2 isn't scoring quite as high as Fable 5.2 on various benchmarks, and I've seen a few complaints that its communication style can be confusing. Theo Browne's review (in the form of a feedback letter he sent OpenAI during pre-release) has this useful example: When this model is working on long tasks, it can pull in a lot of subagents and manage them pretty well. It will then proceed to randomly ask you some weird internal implementation detail bullshit that you could not under any earthly circumstance understand, much less have input on . I sent "/goal make a new level for Outer Wilds". 2 hours in, it's "blocked" because it wanted to ask me "does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?" items.title: Cut generative AI costs: Code for rules, models for judgment
items.description: The biggest cost lever in a generative AI system is whether you call a model at all. We often see teams route every task through a large language model (LLM), including input validation, formatting, and routing. Each call is cheap in isolation, but at production scale these small costs become one of the largest line items in the architecture. Wherever a deterministic rule can do the job, skipping the model saves money, cuts latency, and removes a source of non-determinism. In this post, you learn how to decide whether each step in a workflow needs a model at all. You can then map each option to AWS: deterministic code, a constrained decision call, or a right-sized model on Amazon Bedrock . Why unneeded model calls add up The pattern usually starts in a prototype. A model call works for one step, so it becomes the default for the next. Those steps include validating input, reformatting a request body, and picking a route. At prototype volume, nobody notices the cost. At production volume, unneeded model calls cost you in three ways: Spend grows with request count, even for low-value steps. Latency stacks, because every model call in a chain adds hundreds of milliseconds. Output can vary, because the same input can return a different answer. That makes testing harder and audits slower. Each new model launch then restarts the debate about which model to use. The earlier question, whether the step needs a model at all, goes unasked. Cost guidance, including the AWS Well-Architected Generative AI Lens , often starts at model selection. This post starts one step earlier: Does the step need a model at all? How to decide whether a step needs a model Figure 1 shows the whole decision as a flowchart with three labeled lanes: Runs as code, Questions, and Runs on a model. Take each workflow step through three questions in order, and stop at the first option that meets the step’s requirements: Can a rule check success, such as a format, a schema, a keyword, or a range? If a rule settles only part of the step, a fast path runs the rule first. Can a model write the rule once, such as a regular expression or a JSON schema? Does the step pick one answer from a fixed list, such as a route, a class, or yes or no? If the answer to all three is no, the step is open-ended and runs on a right-sized model. Figure 1: Deciding whether a workflow step needs a model, and which one Consider a customer support assistant. The following table shows how five of its steps go through the chart. # Step Path through the chart Where it runs 1 Check an order number’s format A rule can check success. Amazon API Gateway REST API request validation, or an AWS Lambda function 2 Route a message by intent A rule settles part of it. A keyword match on the fast path resolves messages such as “refund”, and the residual goes to the third question. An AWS Step Functions Choice state that uses JSONata. The residual goes to a constrained decision call. 3 Extract a tracking number from a carrier email A model can write the rule once. It drafts a regular expression, and you review and commit it. Code, as a committed pattern in AWS Lambda 4 Pick one of four support queues for a ticket The answer comes from a fixed list. A constrained decision call. Unsure answers escalate to the right-sized model. 5 Draft a reply to the customer The task is open-ended. The right-sized model, the smallest Amazon Bedrock model that meets the requirements You can use a model when a task is open-ended, ambiguous, or generative: summarizing a document, drafting a reply, extracting meaning from prose. Use deterministic code when the task has a checkable rule: an email format, a schema, an exact keyword, a numeric range. The following table shows what you trade away when you send a rule-shaped task to a model. Property Deterministic code Model call Cost per invocation Typically orders of magnitude lower Per-token, non-trivial at scale Latency Single-digit milliseconds or less Hundreds of milliseconds Correctness on a well-specified rule Exact for the rule as written High, but with a non-zero error rate Auditability The rule sits in source control Harder to explain to an auditor Behavior over time Stable until you change it Changes when you move to a new model version, or when a version is retired A model can also hallucinate and return different answers to the same input. A temperature of 0 makes varied answers less likely, but it doesn’t guarantee identical output. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails help you measure and contain these risks. A rule has neither problem, which is one reason regulated workloads favor rules. A useful test: If you can write the acceptance test as a rule, you can usually write the step as a rule. For more information, refer to Orchestration models: From rule-based to AI-native in AWS Prescriptive Guidance. Decide, don’t generate Most routing and classification steps sit between a rule and open-ended generation. A rule can’t decide every case, but these steps don’t need generated text either. They need one answer from a fixed list of options that you define in advance, like the support queues in the preceding example. Use a component that limits its output to the allowed answers and gives you a signal for when to escalate. Confident answers proceed, and uncertain ones escalate. The AWS Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens describes this tiered, confidence-based escalation . On AWS, you can build it four ways: A small Amazon Bedrock model with structured outputs – The answer is limited to an enum of options, plus an ‘unsure’ option that triggers escalation. This is the model’s own judgment, not a calibrated score, so check it against labeled data before you use it to decide escalation. Embedding similarity – Embed the input with an Amazon Bedrock embeddings model and pick the nearest labeled example. Use the similarity score as an escalation signal, and set its threshold on labeled data. Strands Decider , an experime

items.title: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing
items.description: Today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints. It uses the cache state that the model container reports. It sends each request to an instance that already holds a long cached match for its prompt and isn’t too busy. It’s for teams that serve large language models (LLMs) with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. You turn it on in two places: add one environment variable to your model so the container reports its cache contents, and set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration. Your clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before. Here’s the problem it solves: LLM applications such as chat assistants, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), and agents with long system prompts send many requests that start with the same text. A model keeps the work it did on a prompt in GPU memory, the KV cache, and skips that work when the same start reaches the same instance again. In part 1 of this series , we introduced prefix-aware routing for Amazon SageMaker AI, which sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. Prefix-aware routing infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone, so it can’t tell when an instance has evicted that cache. Prefix-aware routing picks an instance from the request alone. It hashes the start of the request, up to the PrefixLength you configure (bytes of the InvokeEndpoint payload, or characters of the message text for the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API), and sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. It never sees what an instance actually has cached. This works well when every request starts with the same shared text, and less well in two cases: The cache on an instance changes over time. An instance evicts older KV cache entries when its GPU memory fills up, but the router keeps sending matching requests there as if the cache were still warm. A conversation starts out short. In a multi-turn chat, each turn adds to the history. While the request is still shorter than PrefixLength , every new turn changes the text the router hashes, so the next turn can land on a different instance than the one that cached the earlier turns. The turns of a conversation stay on one instance only after the request grows past PrefixLength . In this post, we explain how KV-aware routing works, when to use it, and how to enable, invoke, and verify it on single model endpoints and inference component endpoints. How KV-aware routing works KV-aware routing has three parts: the model container reports what it has cached, SageMaker AI keeps a managed cache index of that state for the endpoint, and the endpoint uses the index to choose an instance for each request. When you turn events on with SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG , the container publishes a KV cache event each time it stores or evicts cache entries, and SageMaker AI uses these events to keep the index current. The index holds only pointers: one-way, truncated hashes of cached content, each mapped to the instance or inference component copy that holds it. It never stores prompts, token IDs, request payloads, or KV tensors. When a request arrives, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks up the tokens in the index. The index returns the instances or inference component copies that hold part of the prompt in their cache, and how much of it each one holds. For example, if instance A holds the cached start of a conversation, the next turn of that conversation goes to A. Because the index matches on tokens rather than a fixed number of bytes, a multi-turn history can match in full as it grows. A request that shares only part of its prompt still goes to the instance with the longest match. The endpoint then picks among these candidates by weighing how much of the prompt each one has cached against how busy it is. A candidate that is too busy is skipped, so if the instance with the longest match is busy, the request goes to the next-best one that is available. If no candidate has a useful match or all of them are busy, the request falls back to load-aware routing, as described in Routing overhead and fallbacks. You don’t configure a concurrency threshold for this, as you do with prefix-aware routing. The index also follows the fleet. When you scale in, entries for removed instances are dropped. When you scale out or an update replaces instances, the new instances start with empty caches, so latency can be higher for a short time. Figure 1: KV-aware routing on a SageMaker AI endpoint. The router looks up the managed cache index and forwards the request to the instance that holds the longest cached match. Each instance reports KV cache events back to the index In Figure 1, the endpoint has three instances, A, B, and C. Each instance runs the same model in its own model container (the AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container listed in Requirements and limits) and has its own KV cache in GPU memory, so each instance holds different cached content: A holds turns 1 to 3 of conversation 1, B holds conversations 2 and 3, and C holds document 7. When turn 4 of conversation 1 arrives (step 1), the router tokenizes it and looks it up in the managed cache index (step 2). The index shows that A holds the first 6,000 of the request’s 6,200 tokens, so the router sends the request to A (step 3), and A only has to compute the remaining tokens. If A is busy, the router sends the request to the least busy instance instead (step 4). KV-aware routing needs a choice of destinations, so it is active only with at least two instances, or at least two copies of an inference component. With a single instance, every request goes to that instance and the setting has no effect. Routing strategies on SageMaker AI With this launch, SageMaker AI offers four routing strategies for real-time endpoints. You set the strategy per production variant in the RoutingConfig of your endpoint configuration. Strategy How it rout

items.title: Govern and discover records with common metadata in AWS Agent Registry
items.description: As organizations build more agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and skills, they need a consistent way to describe, govern, and find them. AWS Agent Registry provides a catalog for registering, approving, and discovering these resources and custom records. Each record carries a name, a description, a protocol descriptor, and an approval status. However, every organization has attributes and facts that it wants to track, and some are unique to that organization, such as its business units, resource owners, risk classifications, and development environments. Organizations want one common definition for each of these attributes, and they want every agent, MCP server, and skill in the registry to carry these facts. Until now, organizations had no way to define these facts in AWS Agent Registry and store them on each record. Custom metadata schemas are now available in AWS Agent Registry. A custom metadata schema is a set of organization-defined key-value pairs that records in an AWS Agent Registry carry. An administrator defines the schema and applies it to the registry, and all records within the registry must then adhere to the schema. When publishers create or submit records, they supply values for the fields specified in the applicable schema, and AWS Agent Registry validates those values against the schema set by the admin. Approvers can rely on the validated values when reviewing a record, and consumers and agents can use them to discover and filter records. Administrators, publishers, security and governance teams, approvers, consumers, and agents all work from a shared set of facts to govern, discover, and understand the resources in their agentic fleet. In this post, we follow the AnyCompany organization publishing an MCP server with custom schema definition, enriching that record, and making it available for discovery by humans or agents. We use an MCP server as the example, but the same steps apply to other record types. How custom metadata works With custom metadata, an organization can use standardized vocabulary for describing its resources. The registry administrator defines the custom metadata schema : field names, types, allowed values, and whether each field is required or optional. The registry enforces the schema on every record, so a field such as environment has the same name and the same allowed values whichever team publishes the record. The schema has common attributes that apply to every record type, and you can add dedicated fields that only apply to specific record types. Each field is Text, Enum, URL, or Boolean. When a record is created or updated, the registry validates the custom metadata against the schema set up by the admin. If a record is created without any custom metadata, AWS Agent Registry saves it as NON_COMPLIANT . A team can save work in progress this way, but it can’t submit the record for approval until it has the required fields and values. If a record includes custom metadata with an unknown field, a missing required field, or an invalid value, AWS Agent Registry rejects it with a ValidationException . GetRegistryRecord returns the record’s custom metadata values and its compliance status. ( COMPLIANT means that the values match the administrator’s schema. It is not an approval. The approvers make that decision.) Discovery APIs also allow filtering records based on custom attributes. What custom metadata makes possible Because teams can describe the AWS Agent Registry records with the same fields and values, the registry can support and scale governance and compliance. Ownership and operations Fields such as environment ( prod , staging , or dev ), businessUnit , ownerTeam , supportContact , and costCenter record where a resource runs, who is responsible for it, and who pays for it. A configuration management database (CMDB) ID links the record to your existing inventory, and a support-tier field sets expectations for anyone who depends on the resource. Security and compliance Data classification, compliance scope such as Payment Card Industry (PCI) or Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), risk tier, scan status, and a scan report URL turn an approval into a check of structured evidence. Your existing scanners, CMDB sync jobs, and classification tools write these values through the API before a record is submitted. You can build your record approval process or automation using these values, as this post shows. Better discovery Custom metadata values are indexed for search. A consumer or agent can combine a natural-language query with specific metadata filters, such as environment=prod AND businessUnit=payments AND securityScanStatus=PASSED . Only approved records are returned, so a record that matches the filters but hasn’t been approved stays out of the results. Figure 1 shows how each role, from administrator to consumer, moves a record through schema definition, registration, enrichment, approval, and discovery. Figure 1: Swimlane diagram showing how a record moves through AWS Agent Registry, by role Walkthrough of an MCP record from registration to discovery AnyCompany operates anycompany-governed-registry , an AWS Agent Registry without auto-approval. Its payments team publishes an MCP record, payments-ledger-mcp , a read-only server for ledger lookups. Existing security and inventory systems enrich this MCP record before an approval function decides whether consumers can discover it. The five numbered steps in Figure 2 match the walkthrough: define, register, enrich and submit, review, then discover. Figure 2: Custom metadata gathers publisher context and values from your existing tools, so approval and search can use the same facts Prerequisites To follow the walkthrough, you need: An AWS account in a supported AWS Region . items.title: Secure OAuth patterns for Snowflake Cortex AI through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: Enterprises today need a clear way to extend their authentication and authorization controls into the agentic layer, often requiring either broad service account permissions or custom-built auth integrations that add operational overhead. When an AI agent running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model) needs to call the Snowflake-managed MCP server (which exposes Snowflake Cortex Agents as one of its tool types) through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the first question enterprises must answer is: how does the agent authenticate? In this post, we walk through three Open Authorization (OAuth) configurations we tested on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Snowflake OAuth (per-user, no external Identity Provider, or IdP), three-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (corporate single sign-on, or SSO), and two-legged OAuth with a third-party Identity Provider (shared service user). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also supports an on-behalf-of (OBO) grant (TOKEN_EXCHANGE) that delivers per-user identity for unattended workloads without a consent prompt. We focus on the three configurations we tested end-to-end, flagging where OBO fits as we go. By the end, you will be able to identify which pattern suits your enterprise scenario. Solution overview Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, connects AI agents to external tool providers through MCP server targets. It targets the Snowflake-managed MCP server, which surfaces Cortex Search and Cortex Analyst as MCP tools that an MCP-aware client can discover and invoke. Rather than acting as a wrapper, the Gateway aggregates the capabilities of its configured targets into a single unified catalog, which it presents to the agent as one tools/list response. The core focus of this post is the outbound authentication for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: how it obtains and presents OAuth tokens to the Snowflake-managed MCP server. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity acts as the credential broker: the Gateway obtains a workload token by calling GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT (because the Gateway uses JSON Web Token (JWT) inbound authentication), then calls GetResourceOauth2Token against the configured provider. AgentCore Identity owns the token vault, the token refresh, and the user-to-token binding, and it fetches, caches, and refreshes tokens automatically. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity supports three OAuth configurations spanning two grant types (authorization_code and client_credentials): Snowflake OAuth : Snowflake acts as its own OAuth authorization server. Each user authenticates directly to Snowflake through the Authorization Code grant (3LO). No external identity provider is needed. Three-legged OAuth using a third-party Identity Provider: Users authenticate through corporate SSO with the Authorization Code grant. Snowflake trusts IdP-issued JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) through its External OAuth security integration. Two-legged OAuth pattern using a third-party IdP: A shared service user authenticates through the client_credentials grant of the IdP. No user interaction or consent is required, which is ideal for machine-to-machine workloads. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity also offers an API-key credential provider (which supports Snowflake Programmatic Access Tokens). We focus on OAuth here for per-user attribution and automatic token refresh. Each configuration uses a credential provider in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity (CustomOauth2, OktaOauth2, or MicrosoftOauth2) and a corresponding security integration on the Snowflake side. Note: We tested these patterns with the Snowflake-managed MCP server using Okta and Microsoft Entra ID. Patterns 2 and 3 (external IdP) follow standard OAuth flows, so they can extend to other OAuth-protected MCP servers, but validate the token claims, scopes, and audience settings for your SaaS provider. Only Pattern 1 is Snowflake-specific, because it relies on Snowflake’s built-in OAuth authorization server. The Snowflake-specific elements are the OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER issuer-lock parameter, the session:role: / session:scope: grammar, BLOCKED_ROLES_LIST, LOGIN_NAME / EMAIL_ADDRESS mapping, and QUERY_HISTORY attribution. If your SaaS exposes its own internal OAuth server, you configure outbound OAuth the same way as Snowflake OAuth. Pattern OAuth grant AgentCore Identity credential provider vendor Snowflake security integration Snowflake query identity mapping Snowflake OAuth – 3LO authorization_code Custom provider (CustomOauth2) TYPE = OAUTH, OAUTH_CLIENT = CUSTOM The real user, with their assigned role 3LO with external IdP authorization_code Built-in provider (such as OktaOauth2, MicrosoftOauth2) TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH + OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER (set with ALTER ACCOUNT / DATABASE / SCHEMA); EXTERNAL_OAUTH_TYPE = OKTA / AZURE / PING_FEDERATE / CUSTOM The real user, with their assigned role 2LO with external IdP client_credentials Built-in provider (such as OktaOauth2, MicrosoftOauth2) or CustomOauth2 TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH + OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER (set with ALTER ACCOUNT / DATABASE / SCHEMA); EXTERNAL_OAUTH_TYPE = OKTA / AZURE / PING_FEDERATE / CUSTOM A shared Snowflake service user Notes: 2LO does not require a built-in vendor. CustomOauth2 with the CLIENT_CREDENTIALS grant can work with your choice of OAuth 2.0 authorization server. When Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway brokers the token (the pattern in this post), Snowflake validates it through the TYPE = EXTERNAL_OAUTH security integration. Setting OAUTH_AUTHORIZATION_SERVER (with ALTER ACCOUNT, DATABASE, or SCHEMA) is what lets direct MCP clients auto-discover your IdP through the Protected Resource Metadata endpoint, and it issuer-locks the MCP endpoint to that integration. items.title: Announcing AI data preparation capabilities in Amazon SageMaker: Build high-quality datasets for model development workflows
items.description: Teams that ship generative AI to production know that a model is only as good as its data. That is why preparing high-quality training and evaluation data comes first. Fine-tuning an open-weight model, running reinforcement learning, or building an evaluation suite all depend on data that is accurate, well-labeled, and representative of your task. For narrow, well-defined tasks, a smaller model customized on clean, task-specific data can often match or exceed the accuracy of a larger general-purpose model prompted into shape, at a lower cost per inference. In practice, though, preparing that data is often the slowest part of the project. Labeled examples are scarce or expensive, and privacy rules limit what you can use. Quality problems such as duplicates, label noise, and answer leakage go unnoticed until a training run disappoints, and every training technique expects data in its own format. As a result, data scientists spend weeks wrangling data instead of building models. Today, we’re expanding Amazon SageMaker AI with new AI data preparation capabilities for model development workflows. You can generate synthetic examples, assess and improve existing datasets, and bring expert feedback into the process through Python SDK APIs and the AWS AI-ML agent skill. You work in your notebook or IDE, with specifications and code that you can inspect and change. Prepare data without hand-building pipelines With AI Data Preparation capabilities, you don’t need to stitch together labeling tools, generation scripts, and validation jobs. Each capability is a standalone building block. You can use one of them on its own or chain them together according to the workflow you want. Auto-labeling: Label data at scale from an unlabeled dataset, a small labeled seed set, or no labels at all. Built-in task types include classification, named entity recognition, extractive question answering, ordinal rating, and summarization, and you can define custom tasks. You describe the task in a short labeling spec, which is validated against your own examples before the full dataset is labeled. For tasks with a fixed set of possible answers, such as classification, named entity recognition, and extractive question answering, a jury of several models labels each row, and their level of agreement becomes that row’s confidence score. Human review: Rows below your confidence threshold go to a review queue in Amazon SageMaker Studio, which uses the open-source Label Studio Community Edition. Outside subject matter experts can access the review app through the link in the partner app box in SageMaker Studio. Reviewer corrections feed back into auto-labeling, and you can generate consensus metrics and labeling reports. Synthetic data generation: Generate training, evaluation, and test data from a specification. You can ground the output in your own seed data and documents, and the service generates a code-based data generation pipeline that you can review, modify, reuse, and scale. Data quality evaluation: Check datasets against your own business rules, built-in metrics, and LLM-as-a-judge metrics. Find duplicates and near-duplicates, and surface issues you didn’t think to check for, such as label noise or answer leakage. Data transformation: Clean and reshape data for your target training technique. Describe the change in plain language and have the code generated for you, use built-in operations such as dedupe, merge, split, and filter, or run your own Python at scale. You work wherever you already work. Use the SageMaker Python SDK directly or provide your coding agent the AI-ML skill in the agent toolkit and let your agent invoke the APIs according to established data science best practices. Describe what you need, and the agent selects and runs the right capability in SageMaker Studio JupyterLab, Kiro, or your local IDE with your coding assistant of choice. For teams building specialized models, the hardest part is often finding enough task-specific data. items.title: Getting AI out of the demo and into businesses globally
items.description: AWS Forward Deployed Engineering is now available in 15 countries including U.S., Mexico, Brazil, Canada, Australia, Singapore, India, South Korea, Japan, UK, Germany, Netherlands, France, Sweden, and Saudi Arabia for commercial and public sector customers; and powered by dozens of built in production-ready accelerators. Every enterprise I talk to has built something with AI that works. A prototype that reads a claim. An agent that resolves a card dispute. A model that answers a customer question in seconds. The prototype works. The demo impresses stakeholders. Then the organization tries to put it into production, and the real problems begin. Production data is messier than the test set. Auditors want to know why the agent made each decision. Volume grows from a pilot group to the whole company. The rules that matter most turn out to live in people’s heads. None of these are model problems. They’re business problems, and they decide whether AI ever pays off. The stretch from demo to production is the last mile, where most AI stalls. It’s also where our teams spend their time. We launched AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) in June to close that gap. Since then, we’ve worked through these problems with commercial and public sector customers in financial services, healthcare, sports, media, retail, and more. Here’s what we’ve learned, and how it shaped what we built. The problem has three layers Model providers, cloud providers, and consulting firms are all embedding engineers with customers. At AWS FDE, we measure success by what remains after our engineers leave: a foundation your team owns, workflows that keep learning, and governance you can trust. Across customers, the hardest problems show up in three layers: the foundation, the workflows, and governance. Each one is harder than it looks, and each one builds on the one before it. That holds whether you’re starting fresh or building on existing systems. On a greenfield build, you can move fast, but there’s no foundation to stand on yet. On a brownfield system, agents must work within decades of data, rules, and integrations. Layer one: A foundation that compounds Before an agent can do useful work at scale, it needs a foundation: identity, security, context, governance, and operational controls. That foundation must be production-ready from day one and shared by every use case that follows. Context is often the biggest gap. Most customers have data spread across systems and no common ontology, the shared model of how the business works that agents need to reason over. Without a shared foundation, the second pilot costs nearly as much as the first. Integrations get rebuilt, and lessons fail to carry forward. Most organizations reach a point where they stop and build the foundation first, so each new use case starts from what the last one built instead of from scratch. We call this the AI reset. Samsung Life Insurance had four affiliates, each building its own AI point solutions from scratch. In 45 days, the FDE team built a governed agentic platform with a single control plane and compliance built in. New agents now deploy through registration and policy assignment instead of a rebuild. Layer two: Automating workflows Next is the work itself: High-volume, rule-heavy processes such as claims processing, know your customer (KYC) reviews, card disputes, loan origination, invoice reconciliation, permitting, and customer service. This is where AI can deliver immediate and measurable outcomes. The payoff is fast, but the knowledge that drives these processes rarely lives in a system. It lives with the people who do the work. The hard part isn’t automation itself. It is uncovering the business rules behind each decision. When an invoice and a purchase order disagree, which record wins? When can an exception clear on its own, and when does it need a person? Experienced employees answer these questions from judgment, and that judgment is rarely written down. Sometimes the knowledge is buried in the systems themselves. Rio Tinto Iron Ore runs one of the world’s most complex mine-to-ship supply chains on a 30-year-old Oracle system. That system has more than 5,000 database tables and 140 applications. Mapping it had been a multi-month exercise. The FDE team built agents that mapped it in weeks, surfacing the dependencies that Rio Tinto’s teams could validate and build against. Mapping what exists is only the start. The biggest opportunities emerge when organizations stop asking how AI can make existing work more efficient and start asking how it can change how work gets done. Layer three: Governance that holds up as everything changes Governance isn’t a phase of the project. It’s part of the architecture. As agents multiply, so do security risks, costs, and decisions you must explain. Every agent needs its own identity, permissions, and audit trail, separate from human identity. And because the models underneath are probabilistic, agents need monitoring that keeps their results predictable and auditable long after launch. The system also must keep working as everything around it changes. Models drift, business rules shift, data formats change, and regulations tighten. New security issues appear, and code falls out of date. As newer models arrive, the instructions and tooling around them will change too. You need evaluations and guardrails that keep agents predictable where they must be and creative where they can be. When governance comes at the end, it becomes the gate that stops production. When it’s built in from day one, it’s what lets your business move fast. Marsh, a leading global professional services firm, needed agents that would hold up under its own audit standards. The FDE team built those controls in from the start, and the first use case reached production about two months after work began. Efficiency gains in the targeted areas have been as much as 70 percent, with some process steps moving from hours to seconds. Marsh has sin

items.title: IEEE Celebrates 10 Years of Incorporating Ethics Into AI Systems
items.description: Policymakers, technologists, and members of the public have raised concerns about the harm AI’s rapid advancement might cause to society. Their concerns include bias, data privacy violations, the spread of misinformation, and losing control of AI agents. Those issues are relatively new to many people, but the IEEE Standards Association has been working for the past decade on ways to prioritize the responsible development of AI systems. In 2016 IEEE SA launched the IEEE Global Initiative for Ethical Considerations in Autonomous and Intelligent Systems (A/IS) and published the Ethically Aligned Design report. EAD ’s mission is to encourage everyone involved in designing autonomous and intelligent systems to prioritize human well-being by applying ethical considerations for the benefit of humanity. Developed by a multidisciplinary community of experts from around the world, the report outlined eight foundational principles for A/IS. They include human rights, people’s well-being, and transparency. More than 100 leading AI ethics experts provided input. EAD ’s Version II report was released in 2017. Both versions solicited public input and received hundreds of pages of feedback, according to John C. Havens , who was the global initiative’s founding executive director, and is now the global director for IEEE Planet Positive 2030 . And by 2019, there were more than 400 contributors and the community continues to grow. “ Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE,” Havens says. “At the time it was released, there wasn’t anything like it.” Since its launch, a series of standards has been developed to provide practical guidelines on designing, building, and deploying technology that prioritizes human values. Several AI ethics certification programs have been introduced. This year marks the 10th anniversary of EAD ’s first draft. To celebrate, IEEE SA recently launched a website , a podcast series , and a blog that reflect on the report’s achievements and impact. Eight guiding principles The word ethics is often used interchangeably with morality , but that is not the case in responsible AI systems design, according to EAD ’s first version. The report includes insights from classical ethics traditions and value-based design methodologies to offer actionable recommendations for engineers developing AI tools. The report established eight foundational general principles for designing autonomous systems: respecting human rights, prioritizing increased well-being as success criteria for development, empowering individuals with data agency to have control over their identity, effectiveness, transparency, accountability, awareness of misuse, and competence for the system creators. The principles shift applied ethics to the design stage of AI systems, compared with being a concern after they’re released, the authors wrote. A suite of standards The IEEE 7000 series of standards has been developed based on EAD ’s framework. Currently the series consists of 29 projects, 11 of which have been published, and more are still being added. They cover topics such as ethical system design model process ( IEEE 7000-2021 ), AI system transparency ( IEEE 7001-2021 ), data privacy ( IEEE 7002-2022 ), algorithmic bias considerations ( IEEE 7003 -2024), the impact on people’s well-being ( IEEE 7010-2020 ), machine-readable personal privacy requirements ( IEEE 7012-2025 ), and systems that mimic human empathy ( IEEE 7014-2024 ). AI ethics certifications IEEE SA offers a suite of ethics in AI programs including IEEE CertifAIEd , which includes two certifications : one for individuals and one for products. The professional certification provides individuals with skills to assess autonomous and intelligent systems for adherence to IEEE’s methodology and ethics criteria. “ Ethically Aligned Design was the first of its kind in the sense of a report that was more than a list of principles and from an organization with the credibility of IEEE.” —John C. Havens, founding executive director of the global initiative The product certification program assesses whether an organization’s AI tool or system conforms to the criteria in the IEEE Ontological Specifications. A CertifiAIEd assessor evaluates the product to ensure it meets the criteria. Upon completion of the assessment, the owner submits it to the IEEE Conformity Assessment Program , which can certify it and issue the certification mark. IEEE SA also recently released its Responsible AI for Children certification program . This program certifies that AI products for children have been independently tested and verified to meet design and ethics requirements. New industry connections group The IEEE Artificial Intelligence Systems (AIS) for Global Flourishing Collaborative Industry Collections group was formed to provide the resources, knowledge, and tools needed to prioritize people’s well-being to developers of AI systems. It has more than 200 members. The collaborative describes its work as a practical, systems-level framework for responsible technology design that translates flourishing into applied methods, metrics, and tools that can be used throughout the AIS lifecycle. The group is establishing guidelines for how to design, evaluate, and govern systems that can measurably improve human well-being and ecological sustainability. Subcommittees are focused on cognition, education, faith, planetary care, spirituality, and other issues. “The group is building directly off the well-being chapter of Ethically Aligned Design and the IEEE 7010 standard (Recommended Practice for Assessing the Impact of Autonomous and Intelligent Systems on Human Well-Being),” Havens says. “That’s on purpose because if human and planetary flourishing aren’t addressed first in design, then human well-being and planetary sustainability are afterthoughts.” Podcasts and blogs To

items.title: Build WhatsApp AI agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: Across Latin America, India, and Southeast Asia, WhatsApp is one of the most widely used messaging applications. That makes it an obvious place to build an AI agent. For many end users, it is how they expect to interact with businesses. However, it is also a genuinely difficult surface to build for, even when your agent already runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . The agent is rarely the hard part. The integration is. Inbound messages arrive as deeply nested, type-dependent payloads that must be authenticated and normalized before your agent can read them. Media such as voice notes, images, and documents each require their own processing pipeline. Beyond message handling, you need conversation memory that survives sessions, durable schedules for reminders, and an authenticated path for external systems to trigger outbound messages. And anything you send more than 24 hours after the end user’s last message must use a pre-approved Meta message template. Wiring that up means configuring more than 10 AWS services and learning a set of WhatsApp system behaviors that most teams discover only by hitting them. None of it is visible to a customer, but all of it has to work. Most teams either build it from scratch or hand the integration to a third-party service. SMART (Social Messaging Agent Runtime Toolkit) is a third option: an open source Python SDK and Terraform stack that gives you the full channel layer. You provide an agent that runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, and SMART handles the rest. One command deploys the entire infrastructure to your AWS account. Teams are already running on SMART with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Webmotors, originally scoped as a two-month engagement, compressed delivery to six weeks and moved their internal team into controlled production ahead of a full launch. Whether you are starting from scratch or migrating an existing agent, you own the agent’s logic. You let SMART handle the channel. The channel layer you don’t need to build The following table compares what each concern costs to build yourself against what SMART provides. Concern Building it yourself With SMART Webhook ingestion Signature verification, nested payloads, a dozen message types Handled, so you receive a clean prompt Media Download, transcribe, store, clean up, and upload outbound files before sending Full lifecycle, both directions Message templates and the 24-hour window Meta approval flow, category rules, tracking which window each conversation is in Declared in YAML, synced by CLI Conversation memory Multi-tier memory, session-break handling Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory, one function call Scheduling and triggers Amazon EventBridge Scheduler wiring, authenticated ingress, routing Built in Infrastructure More than 10 AWS services stitched together One terraform apply Local development Redeploy and tunnel on every change Test locally with the CLI without redeploying The agentic layer Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. SMART builds on two of its main capabilities: AgentCore runtime hosts and scales your agent without you managing infrastructure. AgentCore memory persists conversation history across sessions and deployments, scoped to each phone number automatically. Because AgentCore is framework-agnostic, so is SMART. Strands Agents gets memory wired automatically. LangGraph, Pydantic-AI, or another framework that gives you control over the conversation loop can integrate too. The SDK exposes the same memory and session hooks regardless of framework. You keep full control over the elements that differentiate your product: framework, model, prompt, and business logic. The contract between SMART and your agent is deliberately small. Your agent receives the inbound message and returns text, optionally with rich message attachments. Everything else, session wiring, memory binding, delivery scheduling, is handled for you. The following example is a complete agent.py for a SMART project. The scaffolding command ( socialagent init ) creates the project structure and configuration around it. This file is where your agent logic lives. # --- AgentCore: runtime entry point --- from bedrock_agentcore.runtime import BedrockAgentCoreApp from strands import Agent from strands.models import BedrockModel # --- SMART: channel helpers --- from socialagent_runtime import create_session_manager, socialagent_notify_context, SocialAgentResponse app = BedrockAgentCoreApp() # AgentCore Runtime model = BedrockModel(model_id="us.anthropic.claude-haiku-5-5") #Or any Bedrock model @app.entrypoint async def invoke(payload: dict, context: object = None) -> SocialAgentResponse: agent = Agent( model=model, system_prompt="You are a helpful WhatsApp assistant. Keep replies short.", session_manager=create_session_manager(payload), # AgentCore Memory, pre-wired ) with socialagent_notify_context() as outbound: # SMART: collects outbound messages result = agent(payload["prompt"], invocation_state={"phone": payload["phone"]}) return SocialAgentResponse(result=str(result), outbound_messages=outbound) # SMART: response envelope app.run() The create_session_manager() function binds the agent to AgentCore memory scoped to that phone number, so history survives across sessions and deployments for the memory retention period (7 days by default). The socialagent_notify_context() wrapper is the other pattern worth keeping. Tools sometimes need to send something while the agent is still working, such as a button list or a progress update. Sending it immediately corrupts the conversation history, and the user’s next message fails. The wrapper collects those messages instead, and they go out in order once the turn finishes. Your tools send messages normally and do not deal with the timing. items.title: Reason over time-series data with OpenTSLM on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
items.description: Across industries, decision-making starts with understanding what is changing and why. Industrial organizations collect data that informs decisions across their operations. This data helps prevent production stoppages, diagnose vehicle faults, explain drops in data-center performance, and adjust pricing as supply and demand shift. However, interpreting that data still requires specialist time, and collecting more data does not mean teams can act on it. General-purpose language models like Claude or ChatGPT can help analyze data. However, processing long histories across hundreds of operational metrics as text or images can consume large numbers of tokens, which increases cost. To help organizations act on this data, Aionic Labs is developing temporal foundation models, including OpenTSLM , an open source family of time-series language models (TSLMs). These models interpret operational measurements, from equipment sensor data to supply and demand, alongside context such as maintenance records, market news, and an engineer’s observations. In doing so, TSLMs help systems recognize emerging problems in recent measurements. Experts can then ask follow-up questions to understand what changed and assess how to respond. TimeNet , the shared data infrastructure for time-series data, provides one format and API to find, build, and load the datasets used to train and evaluate these models. Together, they help organizations understand how their systems change and act before problems become costly. OpenTSLM is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart , so you can deploy the model in your own AWS environment. This post explores how Nexthink and Aionic Labs are bringing this capability to proactive IT assistance, then shows how to deploy OpenTSLM and adapt it to your own data using TimeNet. Figure 1. Time-series language models combine numerical measurements with text context and questions. Potential applications span physical and digital systems, with adaptation and evaluation for each task. A customer example: Proactive IT support at Nexthink Nexthink and Aionic Labs are building toward a digital workplace where employees get help before they need to ask for it. At the center is Spark , Nexthink’s personal IT agent, enhanced with time-series language models that connect device telemetry and context to the problems employees experience. Spark turns that understanding into action: it checks the likely issue, guides the employee through an appropriate fix, and follows up on the result. Proactive assistance becomes part of keeping work moving. The workflow combines recent device time-series, such as CPU activity, memory use, available disk space, application stability, and connectivity, with timestamped events and device and software context. The TSLM receives the numerical measurements alongside this text context and interprets how the signals change over the observation window. The TSLM provides Spark with three outputs: State summary: Explains the likely issue and the supporting signal patterns, connecting device behavior with the employee’s experience. Recommended action: Specifies checks to confirm the issue and a practical action for Spark to offer the employee. Expected outcome: Describes the intended improvement and how Spark checks the result. Device telemetry and context support investigation of a range of issues, including slow performance under high CPU or memory load, recurring application freezes or crashes, and files that fail to synchronize. Resource usage, application events, storage measurements, and connection activity provide different pieces of evidence. Combined with device configuration and software versions, they give the TSLM a broader basis for explaining the employee’s experience and directing Spark’s next checks. In the illustrative low-disk example in Figure 2, the TSLM connects declining free space, a rising disk queue, and more frequent application hangs with likely employee symptoms, such as a slow computer or difficulty saving files. Spark checks how much space is left and whether temporary files can be removed using an IT-approved cleanup. If the checks confirm that a cleanup is appropriate, Spark shows the employee what it proposes to remove and asks for confirmation. After the employee confirms, Spark runs the cleanup, checks the space now available, and asks whether the problem has improved. If the issue persists, Spark offers to pass the findings to IT support. TSLMs understand how systems change and help people act on that understanding. For Spark, this means recognizing emerging IT problems and guiding employees toward a solution. The same approach brings time series intelligence to manufacturing, energy, and connected products, turning measurements and context into explanations and intelligent decisions. Figure 2. Illustrative proactive support workflow for low disk space at Nexthink. OpenTSLM generates a state summary, a recommended action, and an expected outcome from device history and context. Spark checks the device, runs an IT-approved cleanup after employee confirmation, and follows up on the result. Solution overview The architecture in Figure 3 provides a reusable deployment pattern for time-series applications. SageMaker JumpStart supplies the model discovery and deployment path. SageMaker JumpStart is a machine learning (ML) model hub that accelerates your ML journey. With SageMaker JumpStart, you can evaluate, compare, and deploy pretrained foundation models (FMs), including the newly available OpenTSLM model. As part of the AWS AI offerings, SageMaker JumpStart provides customizable ML solutions which you can deploy to Amazon SageMaker AI inference endpoints within your AWS infrastructure. It complements Amazon Bedrock , which offers serverless API foundation model inference along with features like customizations, knowledge bases, agents, and guardrails. items.title: AI採用とは？活用できる5業務とメリット・注意点を解説
items.description: 人手が足りない中で、求人票の作成やスカウト文の準備、書類選考に追われ、候補者と向き合う時間が減っていないでしょうか。 採用にAIを使うと、こうした定型業務を減らせます。一方で、学習データの偏りや個人情報の扱いといった新たな課題も生まれます。 本記事では、AI採用とは何か、活用できる業務、メリット、注意点を整理して解説します。 読み終えたときには、自社の採用工程のどこにAIを使い、どこを人が担うかを判断できるようになります。 AI採用とは AI採用とは、求人の作成から選考、面接の記録まで、採用業務の工程にAIを組み込んで効率化や公平性の向上を図る取り組みです。 ポイントは、採用業務をAIに丸ごと任せることではありません。AIが担う作業と、人が判断する作業を分けて設計することにあります。 多くの解説記事が、採用の最終的な合否は人が判断すべきだと指摘しています。AIは、判断の材料を整える役割として使うのが基本です。 AI採用で活用できる業務 AI採用で任せやすい業務は、次の5つです。 求人原稿の作成 スカウト文の作成 書類選考の効率化 応募者からの問い合わせへの対応 AI面接による一次面接の補助 求人原稿を作成する AIは、求人票や募集要項の下書きを短時間で作れます。 職務内容や必要なスキルを入力すると、構成の型に沿った文章を素早く出せます。 出てきた文章は、人が見直す流れにすると品質を保ちやすくなります。たとえば「未経験歓迎」などの表現が応募者の範囲を狭めていないかを、担当者が確認します。 採用担当者は、求人の中身を見直す時間を確保できます。 スカウト文を作成する 候補者ごとに、経歴に触れたスカウト文を作る使い方があります。 文面を一件ずつ書く作業を減らせる点が、この使い方の利点です。 たとえば、候補者の職歴から一つの経験を挙げて関心を示す文面を下書きさせ、人が内容を差し替えてから送ります。定型の文が増えすぎることも防げます。 候補者ごとに丁寧な文面を送りやすくなり、スカウトへの反応を高める土台になります。 書類選考を効率化する 応募書類の要点を整理し、面談の優先順位をつける使い方があります。 大量の応募書類を一件ずつ読む時間を減らせます。 たとえば、職務経歴の要約をAIに作らせ、人が要約と原本を照らし合わせて判断します。要約だけで見送りを決めないことが前提です。 面談すべき候補者を早く見極められるため、選考全体のスピードを上げられます。 応募者からの問い合わせに答える チャットボットで、応募者からの定型の質問に答える使い方があります。 勤務時間や選考の流れに関する問い合わせは件数が多く、担当者の負担になりやすい業務です。 たとえば、選考日程や応募書類の提出方法をチャットで案内する設計が考えられます。担当者の時間外でも答えられるため、応募者を待たせにくくなります。 応募者は答えをすぐに得られ、担当者は面談などの対応に時間を使えます。 AI面接で一次面接を補助する AI面接は、一次面接の質問と回答の記録を自動で行う使い方があります。 同じ質問を全候補者に行えるため、比較の材料をそろえやすくなります。 面接担当者の人数が限られる企業では、一次面接の機会を広げる手段になります。ただし、AI面接の結果は参考情報として扱い、面接官が記録を見直してから判断する流れが欠かせません。 人が面接する候補者を選びやすくなり、面接の質を保ちやすくなります。 AI採用のメリット AI採用のメリットは、主に次の3つです。 業務時間を削減できる 選考の基準をそろえやすくなる 応募者対応を止めずに続けられる 業務時間を削減できる 定型業務の時間を減らし、採用担当者が戦略的な業務に時間を使える点が大きなメリットです。 求人作成や書類整理は、判断よりも手順が中心の作業だからです。 書類整理や文章作成の時間が減れば、候補者との面談や採用計画の見直しに時間を回せます。 採用担当者が採用の質を高める業務に集中できるようになります。 選考の基準をそろえやすくなる AIを使えば、評価の観点を統一しやすくなります。 担当者ごとに判断がばらつく問題を、観点の整理で減らせます。 評価項目を事前に決め、同じ観点で書類を確認する運用が考えられます。観点が統一されていれば、選考の過程を説明しやすくなります。 選考の公平性を高め、候補者にとっても納得感のある選考につながります。 応募者対応を止めずに続けられる 応募者からの問い合わせに、時間を問わず答えられる点もメリットです。 返信が遅れると、応募者が他社の選考に進んでしまうおそれがあります。 夜間に届いた質問に、チャットボットが一次対応する仕組みが考えられます。担当者は翌日、必要な案件だけに対応すれば済みます。 応募者の離脱を減らし、採用の機会損失を防げます。 AI採用の注意点 AI採用を進める前に、次の3点を必ず確認してください。 学習データの偏りを見直す 最終的な合否は人が判断する 個人情報の扱いと候補者への説明を整える 学習データの偏りを見直す AIが学習したデータに偏りがあると、評価の偏りとして表れることがあります。 AIは与えられたデータの傾向をもとに判断するため、過去の偏りがそのまま基準になりやすいです。 たとえば、過去の採用実績だけを学習させると、特定の属性を持つ人が評価されにくくなるおそれがあります。学習に使うデータの内容を事前に点検することが欠かせません。 偏りを人が点検する体制があれば、公平な選考に近づけます。 最終的な合否は人が判断する 採否の判断は、AIの結果だけで決めないでください。 AIは誤りを含む出力を出すことがあり、候補者の人生に関わる判断は人が責任を持つべきです。 たとえば、AI面接の評価を参考情報とし、面接官が記録を見直してから判断する流れが考えられます。判断の経緯を記録として残せば、候補者への説明もしやすくなります。 説明責任を果たしやすくなり、AIへの過度な依存も防げます。 個人情報の扱いと候補者への説明を整える 応募者の個人情報を入力する前に、利用ルールと社内の運用を決めてください。 採用データは機微な個人情報であり、取り扱いを誤ると企業の信用を損ないます。 AIを利用していることを候補者に事前に伝えるとともに、入力してよい情報を社内で定めます。候補者への説明と社内ルールが両方そろっていれば、運用の抜け漏れを減らせます。 候補者の安心感を損ねずに、AIを使い続けられます。 AI採用の導入ステップ AI採用は、次の4つのステップで段階的に進めると定着しやすくなります。 採用課題を整理し、AIに任せる範囲を決める 個人情報の入力ルールを決める リスクの低い業務から試験導入する 結果を検証して運用を見直す ステップ1 採用課題を整理し、AIに任せる範囲を決める 最初に、どの業務に時間がかかっているかを洗い出し、AIに任せる範囲を決めます。 全工程を一度にAI化すると、効果と問題点の切り分けが難しくなります。 求人原稿の作成と応募者の問い合わせ対応の2つに絞って始める方法が考えられます。範囲が小さいと、効果を測りやすくなります。 ステップ2 個人情報の入力ルールを決める 入力してよい情報と禁止する情報を、社内で明確に決めます。 ルールがないと、担当者ごとに判断がばらつき、情報漏えいの原因になります。 候補者の氏名や連絡先は入力せず、経歴を匿名化して使うといった決まりが考えられます。ルールを文書にして全員が見られる状態にしておくと、運用が続きやすくなります。 ステップ3 リスクの低い業務から試験導入する 求人原稿の下書きなど、誤りがあっても影響が小さい業務から試します。 試験導入の段階で問題を見つけ、運用ルールを直せます。 一定期間試したら、人が修正した箇所を記録しておくと、改善点が見えやすくなります。修正の傾向が分かれば、どこまでAIに任せてよいかを判断できます。 ステップ4 結果を検証して運用を見直す 導入後は、効果と問題点を定期的に確認し、ルールを見直します。 一度決めた運用を続けるだけでは、採用の状況や法令の変化に対応できません。 書類通過率や内定承諾率などの指標を決め、改善の前後を比べる方法が考えられます。指標があれば、社内でAI採用の効果を説明しやすくなります。 よくある質問 AI採用に関する質問は以下の3つです。 AI採用は中小企業でも導入できますか AI採用で候補者が不利になることはありますか AI採用を導入すると採用担当者の仕事はなくなりますか AI採用は中小企業でも導入できますか はい、導入できます。大がかりなシステムを入れなくても、チャットAIを求人原稿の作成などに使うことから始められます。 ただし、個人情報の扱いは企業の規模に関係なく確認が必要です。 AI採用で候補者が不利になることはありますか あります。学習データの偏りや、AIの誤った判断によって、特定の候補者が不利になるおそれがあります。 そのため、AIの結果を人が確認する体制が欠かせません。 AI採用を導入すると採用担当者の仕事はなくなりますか 一部の定型業務は減りますが、なくなるわけではありません。 候補者と向き合う面談や採否の判断、採用計画の立案は、人が担う業務として残ります。 担当者は、判断と候補者対応により多くの時間を使えるようになります。 AI採用は人が判断する工程を残して任せる AI採用は、採用業務をAIに丸ごと任せる取り組みではありません。 定型業務をAIに任せ、判断と候補者対応を人が担う設計が、効果と信頼を両立させる基本です。 まずは、自社の採用フローの中で最も時間がかかっている業務を一つ書き出してみてください。その業務が定型作業かどうかで、導入の優先順位が見えてきます。 次に考えるべきは、AIに任せた結果を誰がどの基準で確認するかです。その体制を先に決めておくと、導入後の運用で迷いにくくなります。 The post AI採用とは？活用できる5業務とメリット・注意点を解説 first appeared on AI専門ニュースメディア AINOW .

items.title: AIエージェントの使い方を解説！業務を任せる手順と注意点
items.description: 毎日のメール確認や資料の下調べに時間を取られ、本来考えるべき仕事が後回しになっていないでしょうか。AIエージェントを使うと、こうした作業を一連の流れとして任せられるようになります。 ただし、業務全体をいきなり任せると、誤った情報の採用や意図しない送信が起きるおそれがあります。最初に小さな業務から始め、権限を絞って進める方法を知っておくことが、安全に使い続ける近道です。 本記事では、AIエージェントの使い方を5つのステップで説明し、業務別の活用例と使う前に確認したい注意点を解説します。 読み終えたときには、自社で最初に任せる業務を1つ決め、安全に試し始められる状態になります。 AIエージェントの使い方を5ステップで始める AIエージェントは、次の5つのステップで段階的に始めると失敗が少なくなります。 任せる業務を1つ選ぶ 無料のチャットAIで試す 指示文を具体的にする ノーコードツールで小さく作る 権限を絞って結果を確認する ステップ1 任せる業務を1つ選ぶ 最初に任せるのは、毎日繰り返している定型業務を1つ選ぶことです。 業務の範囲を広げすぎないことが、導入の成否を分けます。 範囲が広いと、AIが何を担当しているのかを把握しにくくなり、結果の確認も難しくなります。たとえば、毎朝のニュースチェックや会議の議事録からTODOを抜き出す作業は、結果の良し悪しを人がすぐ確認できるため向いています。 1つの業務で成果が見えると、次に任せる業務の判断もしやすくなります。 ステップ2 無料のチャットAIで試す いきなり有料のツールを契約する前に、無料で使えるチャットAIで同じ作業を試すことをおすすめします。 チャットAIで試すと、どこまで指示すれば望む結果になるかを手軽に確かめられます。 たとえば、ChatGPTやClaude、Geminiの無料版に議事録の要約を依頼し、出てきた結果を比べてみる方法があります。同じ依頼でもサービスごとに出力が変わるため、自社の業務に合うものを見つける材料になります。 指示の出し方に慣れておくと、エージェント機能を使い始めたときに迷いにくくなります。無料版の利用範囲は変わることがあるため、利用前に各サービスの公式ページで確認してください。 ステップ3 指示文を具体的にする AIエージェントの出来は、指示文の具体性で大きく変わります。 目的や条件が書かれていないと、AIはどこまで進めてよいかを判断できません。 たとえば「議事録をまとめて」と頼むよりも、次のように目的と出力の形を指定したほうが、結果を業務でそのまま使いやすくなります。 以下の議事録から、決定事項、担当者、期限を抜き出してください。 出力は箇条書きで、1項目を1行にまとめてください。 不明な項目は「未記載」と書いてください。 このように型を決めて指示文を保存しておけば、同じ業務を繰り返し任せられます。 ステップ4 ノーコードツールで小さく作る 自分の業務に合わせて仕組みを作るなら、ノーコードのツールから始めるのが現実的です。 プログラミングの知識がなくても、画面上の操作で指示や手順を組み立てられます。 Difyのように、無料プランから試せるツールが複数あります。ただし、無料プランの範囲や料金は変わることがあるため、導入前に各社の料金ページで確認します。 小さな仕組みを自分で組み立てた経験は、社内で次の業務を提案するときの材料になります。 ステップ5 権限を絞って結果を確認する 最初は、AIに読み取りや下書きの作成だけを任せ、送信や削除などの操作は人が承認する形にしてください。 送信や削除は取り消せない場合が多いため、AIの判断を直接外部に反映させないことが基本です。 たとえば社外へのメール送信は、AIに下書きを作らせ、担当者が内容を確認してから送る運用にすると、誤送信のリスクを抑えられます。 この確認を続けると、どの業務までAIに任せてよいかの線引きが自社で見えてきます。 業務別のAIエージェントの使い方例 業務で使う場面は、大きく次の3つに分けられます。 情報収集とリサーチ 議事録からのTODO抽出 下書きの作成 情報収集とリサーチを任せる 指定したテーマの情報を集め、要点を整理させる使い方があります。 集めた情報を整理する手順は、指示文で型にできます。 たとえば「業界の最新ニュースを5件選び、各記事の要点と出典のURLを一覧にしてください」と依頼すると、確認すべき情報が手元に残ります。 出典のURLは、AIの出力をそのまま信じず、人が開いて内容を確かめてから使ってください。集める作業をAIに任せても、事実の確認は人が行うことが前提です。 議事録からTODOを抜き出す 会議の文字起こしから、担当者と期限がある項目だけを取り出せます。 議事録の全文を読み返す時間を減らせる点が、この使い方の利点です。 「決定事項と担当者、期限を表にまとめてください」と依頼すると、会議後の確認作業が短くなります。 抜け漏れを減らせるため、タスクの管理を続けやすくなります。担当者が自分の項目を確認する習慣を合わせて作ると、精度の低い箇所にも気づきやすくなります。 下書きの作成を任せる 社内向けのメール文や報告書の下書きを作らせる使い方があります。 文章の骨組みを作る作業は、AIに任せやすい領域です。 たとえば「先週の進捗を、上司向けに3文で報告する文面にしてください」と依頼します。出てきた文面を人が修正して送れば、文章を一から考える時間を減らせます。 ツールを選ぶ3つの基準 ツールを選ぶときは、次の3つの基準で比べると判断しやすくなります。 任せたい業務に対応しているか 無料で試せる範囲と料金の体系が分かりやすいか 入力したデータの扱いを公式ページで確認できるか 1つ目は、やりたい業務をそのまま任せられるかどうかです。業務に合わないツールを選ぶと、設定に時間がかかり、結局使われなくなります。 2つ目は、無料で試せる範囲を確認することです。試用の段階で使い勝手を確かめてから、有料プランに進むと判断を誤りにくくなります。 3つ目は、入力したデータが社外にどう扱われるかを公式ページで確かめることです。社内の情報を扱う前に、この確認を済ませておくと安心です。
