When evaluated on Allen WTC-11 microscopy at 262k tokens, PACK3D and a matched packed-sequence RoPE control reach comparable Dice on the training layout. Repacking the same validation volumes then costs the packed control 0.048 macro Dice on average, with a loss in all six seeds, while PACK3D changes by 0.0001. On MSD Heart and Spleen, sequence indexing again changes more predictions under repacking, at little cost in Dice. PACK3D also exceeds a parameter-matched 3D U-Net by 0.009 Dice over six seeds, and a full PACK3D layer runs within 7-31% of window-attention latency while adding a global pathway. Geometry, not storage order, should index attention over packed 3D fields. Code is available at https://github.com/amilworks/Pack3D.

items.title: Generating Critic-Guided Synthetic Experience in Latent World Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.39100v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learning from offline datasets is limited in scalability, as collecting new experience is often costly or unsafe in the real world. World models offer an alternative way to generate new experience through a learned dynamics model, yet learning policies in latent space is limited due to compounding errors in imagined rollouts. To this end, we propose using the world model as a local transition generator, leveraging critic guidance to choose actions inside that model to generate synthetic experiences. We study action refinement methodologies, introducing Critic-Guided Synthetic Experience (CGSE) generation in world models. Specifically, CGSE augments an existing offline dataset by sampling candidate actions using an offline policy and refining each to maximize a first-order approximation of the $Q$-function within a trust region. We then use a frozen latent world model to imagine the future state given each updated action, and use the critic to choose the best one, appending this synthetic transition to the replay buffer. Our method requires no additional real-environment interaction or test-time planner, as it generates synthetic experience offline using the world model. On three OGBench manipulation tasks, CGSE improves an offline policy by a relative improvement of $7.1\%$ on the average success rate.

items.title: VideoEditor-MoE: Scaling Complex Video Editing with Mixture of Experts
items.description: arXiv:2611.03043v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Complex video editing requires understanding complex instructions while jointly fulfilling multiple editing requests. Meeting these demands through dense model scaling substantially increases computational cost. We introduce VideoEditor-MoE, the first open-source mixture-of-experts framework for video editing. Beyond sparse MLP-MoE layers, MoE-Attention expands attention capacity through routed key--value experts while preserving global interactions among video tokens. Initialized from a 5B video editing model, VideoEditor-MoE scales to 14B and 56B parameters, with approximately 8B parameters activated per token in both variants. Comparisons with existing methods and two complementary baselines, Explicit-MoE and MLP-MoE, assess its benefits over explicit expert guidance and MLP-only expert architectures. Further analyses demonstrate that all experts remain active and reveal that learned routing responds more strongly to sample content and diffusion noise levels than to human-defined editing categories. Spatial analysis further indicates sensitivity to object-level semantic features. We also identify decoupled weight decay as a strategy for stabilizing expert scaling.

items.title: An Experimental Study of Hybrid Retrieval, NLI and Open-source LLMs for Scientific Claim Verification
items.description: arXiv:2611.03093v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Claim verification is the task of deciding whether a source text supports a claim, contradicts it, or lacks sufficient evidence. Natural Language Inference (NLI) models can judge whether a single sentence supports or contradicts a claim, but they struggle when the evidence is spread across several sentences. Conversely, Large Language Models (LLMs) can reason across sentences, but may draw conclusions the text does not support. In this experimental study, we test whether a conservative fusion rule, labeling a claim Support or Contradict only when both models agree and defaulting to Not Enough Evidence otherwise, combines their strengths. We construct a benchmark of 2,035 claims from SciFact and CliniFact (858 Support, 152 Contradict, 1,025 Not Enough Evidence). We retrieve the top five most relevant sentences per claim using a hybrid of semantic and lexical (BM25) retrieval, which slightly outperforms either method alone. These retrieved sentences are then provided to every verification model. We then compare a DeBERTa-v3-base-mnli-fever-anli NLI baseline against Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B. Qwen3 achieves the highest Macro-F1 (0.7937), followed by Llama 3.1 (0.7204) and Mistral (0.6388), while the NLI baseline reaches only 0.3157. Contrary to our hypothesis, fusion degrades performance, dropping Macro-F1 to 0.7392, 0.6730, and 0.5991, respectively. To understand this decline, we analyze agreements, disagreements, and common error patterns between the NLI and LLM verifiers. Our error analysis shows that NLI and LLM disagreements often result in correct LLM predictions being overturned.

items.title: Model Merging Does Not Require Uniform LoRA Ranks
items.description: arXiv:2611.06486v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Model merging combines separately fine-tuned experts into a single model without retraining. Standard practice trains every expert at the same LoRA rank, which couples the rank choice across experts even though each domain has its own best rank. We show this coupling is a property of the merge method, not of merging. We train 36 experts on three domains (mathematics, instruction following, multilingual) at four ranks and three model scales, then merge with six methods at uniform ranks and at each domain's own best rank. Giving experts different ranks costs averaging and utility-based selection nothing, and gains them up to 1.8 pp of multi-domain accuracy, while the conflict-resolution methods are inconsistent and can lose up to 4 pp. The split has a simple cause. Merging keeps only a fixed share of the pooled spectral components, and methods that choose them by size discard many that would have reduced loss. They also tend to discard the same expert: the instruction adapter has the smallest singular values, so it is dropped almost entirely and IFEval falls by 16 to 25 pp. Choosing components by their effect on loss instead keeps all three experts, and leaves accuracy nearly flat across an 8$\times$ rank range (0.7 pp, against 6.7 pp for TIES at 4B scale). Rank can therefore be chosen per expert whenever the merge operator does not select by magnitude.

items.title: Conflux: Preventing Privilege Escalation with Principal Contexts and System-Level Evaluation
items.description: arXiv:2611.08768v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM agents combine information from multiple principals while acting externally. We formalise privilege escalation (PE) as the system-level security objective: an action may proceed only if every principal that influenced it would allow it. Model-level defences remain probabilistic, so enforcement must sit outside model judgement. We present Conflux, a principal-context defence. Its kernel, ITES, derives authority from provenance and the organisation's existing access-control system and intersects the permissions of every influencing principal. We prove a conditional authority-confinement theorem: under complete mediation, no-laundering provenance, a known non-empty decision context, fresh permission checks, and action binding, the kernel admits no action that escalates privilege with respect to any recorded influencing principal. The theorem covers the represented value-influence fragment; control influence from tool, branch, recipient, or plan-step selection remains a refinement obligation. Conflux extends the kernel with independent policy ports, argument-aware authorisation, disclosure, consent, delegation, restriction, and exposure planning. We describe two system- level evaluators. SLED is a black-box evaluator: it exhaustively explores a declared finite model of a defence up to a bound. SLED-V is a white-box evaluator: it checks a serialisable intermediate representation against security and provenance properties. The evidence is bounded and partial. The appendix reports retained AgentDojo, SLED, and SLED-V results, including the limits of those runs. No result in this paper is an unbounded deployment guarantee.

items.title: Goodhart in the Planner: Sampling-Based Control Exploits Rewards Learned from Human Preferences
items.description: arXiv:2611.09670v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robots increasingly plan by searching against a reward model learned from human preferences; we measure what this search does to the true objective. On HalfCheetah and Hopper with crowd-sourced labels, and on Meta-World drawer-open and plate-slide with synthetic labels and blind labels from the two authors, harder MPPI search cuts true return by up to 76% while held-out label accuracy stays at 0.75-0.97: with human labels the drawer opens in 0 of 20 runs, against 10 of 10 for the cloned policy the planner starts from. The effect persists with a learned dynamics model and with an image scorer. True return roughly follows how far the planner's weights move from its proposals ($\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}}$), and best-of-$N$ action selection with a verifier trained on synthetic labels falls below a single noisy action. We prove that $\chi^2$-regularized MPPI at a temperature set by the scorer's error spread on the proposals is worst-case optimal, that no gain can be certified once that spread exceeds the scorer's own, and that an episode's return splits exactly into per-step terms, only some of which the guarantee covers. Calibrated from 100 proposal pairs ranked by true return (an oracle), this rule is the safest fix we test: it keeps on average 86-94% of the cloned policy's return on drawer-open and plate-slide, though it is cautious on window-open, where search helps. Calibrated from a person's own comparisons, it cannot detect a bias the scorer shares with that person; a second person, or correcting for pairs people cannot tell apart, limits the damage.

items.title: Jais 3: Introducing Arabic-centric Agentic AI
items.description: arXiv:2611.10224v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present Jais 3, a fleet of six open, Arabic-centric agentic language models ranging from 0.9B to 375B parameters. Jais 3 is built to complete tasks for Arabic speakers, not only to answer questions in plain text: it is trained to plan multi-step tasks, call tools and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, operate a terminal, search the web, and read, edit, and produce PDF, spreadsheet, and presentation files, while communicating with the user in Arabic. Instead of pretraining from scratch, we adapt each model of the fully open K2 Horizon fleet to Arabic through continual pretraining, followed by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), final token preference optimization (FTPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We combine natural Arabic text with translated, transliterated, and synthetic Arabic, and replay the base model's own training data to keep its reasoning, agentic, and English abilities. Jais 3 covers Modern Standard Arabic and the major regional dialects, follows instructions with Arabic-specific constraints, and inherits the 512K-token context window of K2 Horizon (all models except the 0.9B). To our knowledge, its 375B model is the largest open Arabic-centric language model to date. For evaluation, we revisit how Arabic models are assessed, moving to fully generative evaluation on audited Arabic benchmarks. Across model sizes, Jais 3 matches or outperforms open-weight models of comparable size on Arabic and agentic benchmarks, with particularly strong agentic capabilities and Arabic instruction following, and far fewer hallucinations. We release the weights and the checkpoints from every training stage of all six models, together with samples of the training data, the data recipes and training configurations, the training logs, the audited benchmarks, and the evaluation code.

items.title: Longtail-SWE: High-Quality SWE Tasks for Underrepresented Languages
items.description: arXiv:2611.10304v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Challenging repository-level benchmarks remain limited for many programming language ecosystems, where filtering scarce candidates with ambiguous descriptions or defective tests can discard valuable engineering problems. We introduce Longtail-SWE, a benchmark of 202 issue-resolution tasks across 13 languages with limited coverage in existing repository-level benchmarks: Clojure, Dart, Elixir, Erlang, F#, Haskell, Julia, Kotlin, Lua, OCaml, R, Scala, and Swift. Its construction uses a solver-judge-repairer pipeline: a solver attempts each candidate task, and a judge reviews the task together with the solver's trajectory and test results to guide revisions to tests and task descriptions. These revisions aim to correct tests that reject valid alternative implementations or accept incorrect solutions while retaining challenging tasks and preserving their intended requirements. We evaluate nine model configurations, including frontier models, and analyze task-solving performance, consistency across repeated attempts, and resource usage. We release all benchmark instances, executable environments, complete construction and evaluation tooling, and agent trajectories, together with an additional set of easier tasks to support evaluation of smaller models.

items.title: Quantitative Assessment of Crystal Structure Prediction
items.description: arXiv:2611.10380v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) aims to predict a material's 3D structure from its chemical composition, with applications from energy storage to biomedical devices. Despite its importance, existing evaluation frameworks suffer from key limitations: they rely on threshold-sensitive or incomparable metrics, focus predominantly on geometric performance while overlooking physical plausibility, and fail to account for polymorphism, where a chemical composition can crystallize into multiple stable structures. In parallel, recent Symmetry-Informed CSP (SICSP) methods often report results alongside standard CSP baselines while receiving crystallographic templates at inference, which constrain the search space and make SICSP a fundamentally different task. To address these limitations, we introduce an Orientation-invariant, Polymorph-Aware, Large Benchmark (OPAL-Bench) that evaluates CSP and SICSP as separate tasks. We evaluate 7 CSP and 2 SICSP methods under OPAL-Bench across 4 datasets using threshold-free geometric and physical distance metrics. Our results show that no method dominates across all metrics, and that geometric performance is not strongly correlated with physical plausibility. We also release OPAL-CSP, an SE(3)-equivariant flow-matching baseline for the CSP track that performs competitively on geometric metrics and ranks among the best on physical ones. By unifying geometric and physical metrics under a polymorph-aware protocol, OPAL-Bench enables a more comprehensive assessment of generative quality in CSP.

items.title: Imperfectly Imperfect: Evaluating Graded Cognitive Diversity in LLM Persona Simulations
items.description: arXiv:2611.10508v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used as synthetic participants in social, behavioural, and decision-making research, yet it remains unclear whether they can express graded cognitive diversity as assigned when engaging in simulated behaviour. We introduce a cognition-suite evaluation that tests whether simulated populations reproduce human variation in reasoning, self-reported traits, their associations, and downstream behaviour. Agents conditioned on synthetic or human-derived profiles of cognitive reflection, Need for Cognition, and Big Five personality answer the same suite as a cohort of 473 adults: two newly assembled tests, a Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) and a Behavioural Reflection Test (BRT) whose decision scenarios measure reflection in behaviour, alongside an established CRT and the two trait questionnaires. Across seven full-battery simulation runs of four models, agents recover Need for Cognition and Big Five trait distributions on self-report questionnaires, but fall short on simulating diversity of cognitive task performance and downstream behaviours. In the four Claude Sonnet 4.6 runs, every agent scores full marks on both CRTs, whatever reflection level its persona was assigned. In the other three runs agents make intuitive-lure errors (the tempting wrong answers CRT items invite), but 49 to 85% score full marks, against under 10% in the human sample. Claude Sonnet 5 comes closest to people's item-by-item pattern of lures; the other two runs give fewer lures and vary less between items. In the BRT scenarios, every run over-produces 8 to 11 of 15 coded behaviours by at least 20 percentage points, and people's links between reflection and behaviour carry over only in part. Useful synthetic populations must preserve not only trait descriptors but the structured variation in reasoning, error type, and behaviour those descriptors are meant to organise.

items.title: Evaluating Jev on Arabic: Comparing Decision Models and LLMs Across Arabic Tasks and Dialects
items.description: arXiv:2611.10802v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: How does Jev compare with other systems on Arabic tasks, and how does its performance change between Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and dialects? We evaluate 67 systems, including 47 decision models and 20 large language models (LLMs), on 43 tasks across 9 task families using a shared zero-shot protocol. The Arabic-focused frozen suite includes English controls in three parallel resources, which we also remove in a separate descriptive comparison. Jev 1.14.0 achieves a mean task-primary metric of 69.24 on a scale multiplied by 100, compared with 68.77 for Jev 1.13.0 and 71.81 for Gemma-4-31B, the highest-scoring system on this aggregate. Removing the recorded English controls, repeated cross-task items or both leaves the full system order unchanged. Relative performance and gains between Jev versions vary across task families. In content-matched comparisons within Jev 1.14.0, pooled dialect-minus-MSA accuracy gaps range from -7.94 to -0.35 percentage points across four datasets; dialect-specific results show larger variation, and SIB-200's source-clustered interval includes zero. Paired contrasts with Jev 1.13.0, Gemma-4-31B and Jais-2-8B show a larger Palestinian banking penalty for Jev 1.14.0 than for either LLM under simultaneous uncertainty; the other gap contrasts remain inconclusive. These descriptive findings show why aggregate scores should be read alongside task-family results, coverage and matched language comparisons. They do not establish a general model ranking for dialect robustness or explain the causes of the observed gaps.

items.title: Agent Self-Improvement with Frozen Weights: The Added Value and Limits of Failure Traces
items.description: arXiv:2611.11342v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We evaluate whether an AI agent's harness, the notes around its model, can learn from the agent's failure traces beyond a matched search that never sees them. It can, but less than it looks. We tested an open 9-billion-parameter model with fixed weights; a larger teacher model wrote its notes. On generated customer-service decisions, where both note writers were told the target rules, notes based on the agent's mistakes improved accuracy by 4.0 percentage points over notes from the same process with the mistakes withheld. That process alone, trying and keeping better-scoring notes, reached about 60% of the total improvement. In full customer-service conversations the same notes showed no demonstrated improvement. Separately, a strict screen of single lessons admitted two customer-service lessons, still awaiting tests on new data, and one tool-use lesson, written without seeing the agent's mistakes, which showed no demonstrated gain on new tool-use tasks. A neutral note with no procedure scored higher than the learned lessons (exploratory). A blind audit judged 146 of 240 tool-use test items defective.

items.title: Steering Emergent Behavior in Multi-Agent LLM Systems via Information Networks
items.description: arXiv:2611.11714v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in groups, each pursuing an individual objective while jointly determining system performance. If an operator controls which agent observes which other agent, but not their payoffs or messages, how should observations be structured to raise collective welfare? We make the information network (who observes whom) a design object, decoupled from the fixed interaction network over which agents act. Ten identical LLM agents play repeated group-decision games; by default each observes only an anonymous summary of the group's previous-round outcome, and a manager with a fixed budget adds directed observation links that reveal peers' past actions. Across 1,080 episodes and six games spanning coordination, anti-coordination, social dilemmas, and discovery, we ask how much information to share and, at a fixed budget, who should observe whom. Disclosure creates behavioral coupling: observation acts as a contagion channel whose welfare effect depends on the alignment between individually attractive behavior and the collective objective. First, the value of information is alignment-contingent: more peer information tends to help or be neutral when individual behavior is aligned with the collective goal, but under free-riding or congestion externalities it amplifies collectively harmful behavior; in a public-goods game the group does best with no information at all. We read this sign separation as a cross-game regularity within one controlled LLM population, not a model-invariant law. Second, at a fixed budget, who observes whom matters primarily when coupling is harmful: a modular "barbell" that lets sub-populations entrench harmful behavior is reliably the worst wiring, reversing the network-reciprocity intuition from human evolutionary game theory. These results argue against a default of full transparency for agent collectives.

items.title: Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids (DASH): Latency-Agnostic Scaling of Vision-Language-Action Models for Humanoid Manipulation
items.description: arXiv:2611.11854v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a vision-language backbone with an action head, but in closed-loop control the backbone sits on the control-critical path: while it computes, the robot keeps moving, so each executed action is conditioned on an increasingly stale observation. A larger backbone therefore directly blocks reactivity, especially in humanoid dexterous manipulation. We present DASH, a Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids that removes this coupling. DASH splits the policy into a slow vision-language model (System 2) and a fast flow-matching action head (System 1) that run as concurrent processes over the LCM communication protocol, so the control rate is set by the action head alone, independent of backbone size. The action head fuses stale semantics from a frozen backbone with fresh vision from its own ResNet encoder, desynchronized training exposes it to the staleness it meets at deployment, and an adaptive temporal aggregator aligns overlapping action chunks under variable inference latency. On an asynchronous RoboTwin benchmark that charges inference latency in simulated time, DASH holds 20 Hz control rate from 0.8B to 8B backbones while the synchronous rate falls from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz, with higher success at every size. On a real humanoid with dexterous hands, DASH achieves clearly higher pick-and-place success than the synchronous pipeline.

items.title: CARE-PO: Controllable Tool-Call Efficiency for LLM Agents
items.description: arXiv:2611.12125v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: External tool calls are a major running cost of an LLM agent, while its training objectives align almost exclusively with task completion. In a step-level diagnosis of Qwen3.5 trajectories at two model sizes on GAIA, a long-horizon tool-use benchmark, we find that most contain removable calls, at a similar rate at both sizes. Some methods add an efficiency reward to the objective to reduce the call count, but introduce problems of their own: the anchor they price calls against is computed from the policy's own rollouts (e.g., the group's shortest correct rollout) and so moves with the policy; training can drift toward a collapsed policy that issues no tool call at all, a degeneracy seen in published reports and in our 27B baseline; and a training run delivers a single operating point, so the user cannot trade efficiency against capability. We present CARE-PO (Controllable Anchored Relative Efficiency Policy Optimization) to mitigate these problems. The efficiency reward prices calls against a reference budget anchored to the task's own difficulty and fixed before training. Injecting a successful trajectory from the training data into each online GRPO rollout group and charging for evidence a trajectory never gathers ease the drift toward a collapsed call count. Shaping the cost curve by an effort tag in the prompt yields an efficiency and a capability operating point from a single training run. On GAIA, five of the six operating points across three model sizes improve on their base model in success rate and call count at once. On four held-out multi-hop benchmarks the result is size-dependent: at 27B and 4B success rate is held or raised at a lower call count, while at 9B both operating points trade success rate for fewer calls. The call count remains well above zero throughout training at all three sizes.

items.title: Visible Tails: Characterizing Adaptation to Unknown Moments in Heavy-Tailed Bandits
items.description: arXiv:2611.12140v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Heavy-tailed bandit learners must tell a poor arm from an arm whose favorable rewards have not yet appeared. We characterize this obstruction through a scale of one-sided visibility conditions on the optimal reward law: the mean hidden in a rare event is at most a constant multiple of a retained central moment. A quantile-trimmed UCB index that is given the visibility constants attains arm-specific moment rates at every exponent, with no lower bound on the exponent. Conversely, every strategy with a fixed exploration budget has polynomial regret on each law that violates the corresponding condition. For the variance benchmark we determine the order of both budget constants in the visibility level. The frontier depends on the largest exponent the benchmark promises, and the resulting classes are strictly nested. The same index has logarithmic expected regret when rewards are integrable, with a coefficient that can be exponential in the inverse gap.

items.title: Transactional Data Change for Real-Time Analytics in Lakehouses
items.description: arXiv:2611.12169v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Real-time data analytics has become a key demand for lakehouses. It requires propagating data changes from the data source to the lakehouse in real time, while ensuring ACID guarantees and minimizing resource consumption and impact on analytical query performance. This is highly challenging for a data system according to the RUM conjecture, especially given the read-optimized immutable file storage layer in lakehouses. Existing lakehouses offer only git-style catalog version control on a single table, and they trade data freshness, query performance, and/or resource efficiency to achieve a barely acceptable data-change throughput. In this paper, we propose a novel data synchronization framework, Retina, that enables real-time, cost-efficient, query-performant, and fully transactional data changes in lakehouses. We implement and open-source Retina. Evaluations show that Retina delivers 10-millisecond-level data freshness and over 3.2 million row/s linear-scalable data-change throughput with low resource consumption and query-performance overhead, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art lakehouse systems and lake-compatible HTAP databases.

items.title: HumanSightBench: A Benchmark for Human Visual Perception in MLLMs
items.description: arXiv:2611.12305v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong performance on knowledge-intensive and reasoning-based vision-language benchmark datasets, but still struggle to solve the visual questions that people can solve easily. Evaluating the differences between MLLMs and human-level visual perception is challenging due to end-to-end evaluation which combines various skills, or because we are uncertain if individual items are valid. Specifically, observed errors may reflect visual perception, language priors, background knowledge, question ambiguity, and underspecified answers. Our guideline for HumanSightBench is that we construct items that are human-easy by construction and model-hard by evaluation. HumanSightBench contains 2,876 visual questions with short answers across 7 top-level perceptual categories and 21 subcategories. We only include items that pass five inclusion gates: question clarity, answer uniqueness, visual grounding, human solvability, and text-only shortcut filtering. According to the protocol, errors are defined as incorrect answers on human-validated visual tasks with the evaluated interface. The inclusion gates are intended to reduce confounds from ambiguity and external knowledge. The best pass@3 score is 65.6% across eight evaluated MLLMs. No evaluated model exceeds 27.5% on Counting. These results identify capability gaps that are hidden by overall scores and can help future training experiments and held-out evaluation.

items.title: Production MLOps at GS Caltex with Amazon SageMaker Canvas, part 1
items.description: GS Caltex uses Amazon SageMaker Canvas and Amazon SageMaker Pipelines to connect process engineers’ models to production workflows. The South Korean energy and chemical company divides model development and operations between engineers with complementary skills. Process engineers build and validate models in SageMaker Canvas without writing code, drawing on their process knowledge. Machine learning (ML) engineers configure SageMaker Pipelines workflows for deployment and scheduled inference. Moving assets from SageMaker Canvas into SageMaker Pipelines still required integration work. ML engineers had to set data paths for production, supply the model configuration, and connect preprocessing and inference jobs. GS Caltex automated this handoff while reusing the assets created in SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex reports that its ML engineers now deploy models within a few hours, compared with about a week before. The company runs batch inference every 30 minutes, reducing the need for continuously running endpoints. GS Caltex reports that this has meaningfully lowered its inference costs. This post explains how GS Caltex connects SageMaker Canvas to SageMaker Pipelines and reuses validated preprocessing flows and models in production. Solution overview The machine learning operations (MLOps) workflow has two paths: preparing a new model version for deployment, and running batch inference with the deployed model. From a validated model to a repeatable workflow You can use SageMaker Canvas to prepare data visually, build models, and generate batch predictions. You can also register validated models in Amazon SageMaker Model Registry from SageMaker Canvas. GS Caltex built a separate handoff process to turn these assets into executable SageMaker Pipelines steps. Process engineers understand the variables and data behind a process and assess whether a model’s predictions are useful. ML engineers turn the resulting assets into production jobs and manage model versions and execution history. Area What is prepared in SageMaker Canvas What is managed in the production workflow Data preparation A preprocessing flow built with Data Wrangler Preprocessing jobs in Amazon SageMaker Processing Model development A trained model and evaluation results Model versions and approval status in Model Registry Prediction Validation of model predictions Batch inference every 30 minutes using an approved model Operations Development and validation of individual models Step execution history, stored results, and failure handling Reference architecture The following diagram shows how process engineers hand off SageMaker Canvas assets to ML engineers for deployment and scheduled inference. ML engineers use Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for preprocessing flows and Model Registry for model versions, then schedule pipeline runs through Amazon EventBridge. Figure 1: SageMaker Canvas assets connected to a SageMaker Pipelines workflow for scheduled batch inference ML engineers receive the preprocessing flow and model from SageMaker Canvas and review the data formats and prediction results. After that review, they approve the model in Model Registry and deploy it. This preparation takes place when a new model version is deployed. Subsequent inference runs reuse the deployed model. Amazon EventBridge starts each scheduled run. SageMaker Pipelines prepares the input data from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), runs preprocessing and SageMaker Batch Transform , and stores the results in S3. ML engineers can inspect step status and Amazon CloudWatch logs to monitor the workflow. The production pipeline reuses the preprocessing logic and trained model created in SageMaker Canvas. ML engineers configure the input and output paths, set the order of execution, and write the code that connects approval and scheduling to the workflow. Prerequisites Before you begin, prepare the following: A model built and evaluated in SageMaker Canvas , along with its Data Wrangler preprocessing flow CSV data for inference and an S3 bucket to store the files. A SageMaker execution role and an Amazon EventBridge role with permission to start the pipeline A Python environment with Boto3 and SageMaker Python SDK 2.x installed. The full reference implementation is available in the GitHub repository . The code examples in this post focus on the connections between components. The repository uses a sample loan classification model, so adjust the configuration to match your model’s input and output formats. Technical implementation The following steps cover preprocessing reuse, model approval and deployment, pipeline construction, and scheduled inference. 1. Run the SageMaker Canvas preprocessing flow with SageMaker Processing A preprocessing flow created with Data Wrangler in SageMaker Canvas records the data sources and transformation steps. To set up the reference implementation, export data to Amazon S3 using SageMaker Processing, then retrieve the job settings and the .flow file used by that job. In the export settings, turn off Auto job configuration and select SageMaker Processing . After the export starts, open the Processing job details on the Amazon SageMaker AI console. Record the container image URI, the S3 URI of the input named flow , the execution role, and the output settings. Use these values to configure the pipeline step that runs the .flow file. The SageMaker execution role must have permissions to read the required S3 data, write the results, and access the container image. Choose the instance type and count based on the volume of data you need to process. Keep the preprocessing logic validated by the process engineer, and adjust the data sources, paths, and other settings for the production environment. items.description: Release: datasette-leaflet 0.3 OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a referrer header . Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy. datasette-leaflet is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It now sets the referrer policy on the tile requests themselves to strict-origin-when-cross-origin , passing the host but not the full path to the page. Tags: leaflet , datasette , openstreetmap

items.title: Route coding agent requests to the right model on Amazon Bedrock with NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard
items.description: Coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex CLI work in tasks. A developer asks for a change, and the agent reads files, edits code, and runs tests until the work is done. One task can take a few model calls or dozens. What the developer pays for is the task, not one call. The price per token alone doesn’t tell you what a whole task costs. The total depends on how many turns a model needs, how much history each turn replays, and how often a task has to be retried or never finishes. You pay for every attempt, including attempts on tasks that never finish. So when you route a coding agent’s requests between models, judge the routing by cost per solved task: the total cost of your runs divided by the number of runs whose tests pass. NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard is an open source library that helps an AI agent choose which model handles each request. You define the models that it can use and the strategy that it follows. Its LiteLLM integration supports two strategies. Stage routing reads the recent tool activity and results in the request history, and then picks one of two candidate models. Random routing picks from the configured models, with optional weights, for traffic splits and A/B comparisons. Another option you can explore is LiteLLM, who also recently shipped a native built-in Switchyard stage router as an auto-router strategy. In this post, you use the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to deploy LiteLLM, an open source gateway for large language models (LLMs), with the Switchyard routing plugin in your AWS account. LiteLLM calls the models on Amazon Bedrock . You then use the sample’s benchmark runners to measure cost per solved task for a routed model group and for single-model baseline groups, so that you can evaluate routing against your own workloads. Note: The sample installs switchyard-server 0.3.0 from crates.io and runs the published LiteLLM v1.102.0 image. NVIDIA documents switchyard-server 0.3.0 as a demo and evaluation component, and its configuration can change between releases. This sample uses the experimental Switchyard LiteLLM integration and its configuration and APIs may change between releases. This is sample code, for non-production usage. Work with your security and legal teams to meet your organizational security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before deployment. Deploy the sample in a non-production account and test it before relying on it. Solution overview Figure 1 shows the architecture of the solution. LiteLLM and the Switchyard plugin run in one container image on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate , in private subnets. Figure 1: Solution architecture A request flows through these steps. The numbers match the diagram. The coding agent sends an OpenAI-compatible request with the model field set to switchyard , the LiteLLM model group that Switchyard routes, and the shared gateway key in the Authorization header. The endpoint is your hostname over HTTPS, with an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate on the load balancer, and only the IPv4 CIDR range that you allow can reach it. With a hosted zone in Amazon Route 53 , Route 53 resolves the hostname to the load balancer. AWS WAF filters the request with IP reputation, known bad input, and per-IP rate-limit rules. The Application Load Balancer forwards only /v1/chat/completions , /v1/models , and /health/liveliness to the ECS task in a private subnet, and answers every other path with 404. The task runs one container: LiteLLM with the embedded Switchyard plugin. LiteLLM validates the gateway key and calls the plugin to pick a model. Stage chooses between a capable model and a lower-cost efficient model. It reads the tool activity and results in the request history, so the agent must send the full conversation history. Random chooses from a weighted pool. Neither strategy calls a judge model. LiteLLM calls the selected model through the Amazon Bedrock Converse or ConverseStream API, with the task’s AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role for credentials. The call goes through an Amazon Bedrock Runtime interface endpoint in the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) , so inference traffic stays on the AWS network. The response or token stream returns through LiteLLM and the load balancer. The x-litellm-model-name response header names the model that answered. The response body’s model field stays switchyard . LiteLLM listens on port 4000 in the container and is the load balancer’s target, and the task’s security group admits only the load balancer. The path allowlist keeps the LiteLLM admin UI, API docs, and key management routes unreachable. Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) holds the gateway image. AWS Secrets Manager generates the secret behind the gateway key, and the container adds the sk- prefix when it starts. The task definition passes the profile files in LITELLM_CONFIG_TEXT and SWITCHYARD_CONFIG_TEXT , and the startup script writes them to /tmp before it starts LiteLLM. Logs go to one Amazon CloudWatch log group, / /litellm , which keeps them for 30 days, and Container Insights collects metrics. The VPC spans two Availability Zones, and one NAT gateway provides outbound access for image pulls and other AWS services. The plugin supports Stage routing, which needs exactly two candidates, and Random routing, which needs at least two and splits traffic by weight for A/B tests. Classifier-backed strategies, such as Task and Composite routing, need intermediate model calls that this integration doesn’t support. See the Switchyard routing overview for the full catalog. Prerequisites To follow this walkthrough, you need the following: A non-production AWS account with Amazon Bedrock access to Claude Opus 5.5 and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super 120B. The pair has been tested in US East (N. Virginia). For other AWS Regions, check Regional availability by models and tool-calling support. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2 with configure

items.title: Architecture patterns for fast session startup on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
items.description: Agents today review code, process claims, and run unattended for hours. Many also sit behind interactive experiences where a person waits for the first response. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime gives these agents a fully managed, serverless environment: each session runs in its own isolated microVM, the platform scales to zero when there’s no work, and you only pay for the resources your sessions consume. AgentCore runtime with platformVersion set to “V2” changes how sessions start. Instead of initializing your container for every session, it prepares your environment once, snapshots it, and restores that snapshot for each new session. Session start times are faster and more consistent. V2 also reclaims memory your sessions don’t use, so your bill tracks what your agent uses. For most agents, switching to V2 is all it takes. Some agents need restructuring to get the full benefit, and for chat and voice experiences even 2 seconds is too slow. This post explains how V2 starts a session, how to measure session start time, and how to keep work off the first request, including build hooks, which AgentCore runtime now supports. We cover four patterns, from changes to your agent’s code to starting sessions before users need them. Which pattern do you need? Your situation What to do Section A new session in about 2 seconds is fine Switch to V2 and do all initialization before app.run() Keep work off the first request Your agent needs large files, a CLI, or a browser early, and can’t hold them in its process Add a build hook to load and prime them while the snapshot is built Working with hooks You need sub-second, and users engage before they send their first request (opening the app or a chat window) Start the session in the background when the user engages Pre-warm on user engagement How V2 starts a session AgentCore runtime runs each session in a new microVM. On V1, AgentCore pulls your container image from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), starts the container, and runs your initialization code before it can process the first request. The image pull dominates, so cold start grows with image size. V2 does that work once. When you create or update a runtime, AgentCore runtime starts your container in a fresh microVM and waits for the first healthy ping ( GET /ping ), which must arrive within 120 seconds. It then clears the operating system’s file cache, to keep the snapshot small, freezes the microVM, and stores its memory and disk as a snapshot. This is a change from V1: Every create or update now takes a few minutes while the snapshot is built. In this post, init means everything your agent does before /ping reports healthy. With the AgentCore Python SDK, that’s everything before app.run() . If you run your own HTTP server, in Node.js or another language, report healthy only after your initialization finishes. Figure 1: Build, once per create or update When a new session arrives, AgentCore restores the snapshot into a new microVM. Your process resumes exactly where it was frozen, with its imports, objects, and clients in place. Files from your image are loaded lazily: each block is fetched the first time a session reads it. Figure 2: Invoke, every new session Three facts follow from these flows, and the rest of this post builds on them: Memory comes back whole. Anything your process held at snapshot time, and anything in a RAM-backed file system such as /dev/shm , is available at memory speed from the first access. File reads don’t carry over. The file cache is cleared before the freeze, so reading a file during init doesn’t make it fast in a restored session. Image files are fetched on first read. The first read of a block comes from snapshot storage and is then cached closer to the host. The following table shows what that means for the work a typical agent does, depending on where it does it: Work Done during init Done in the handler Import libraries In memory when the session starts Read from the image in every new session Create clients (for example, boto3 ) Restored with endpoint and credential resolution done. Sockets reconnect on first use Built from scratch in every new session Open network connections Stale after the restore. Close them before the snapshot Opened fresh Load static data from the image and keep it in an object In memory when the session starts Read from the image in every new session Read a file from the image without keeping the data No effect, because the file cache is cleared Read from the image in every new session If you know AWS Lambda SnapStart, this will feel familiar. Marc Brooker’s post on how SnapStart loads snapshots and the SnapStart priming strategies post are useful background. Everything in the table assumes your agent can keep what it needs in its own process. That isn’t always possible. A CLI that runs as a separate process and exits, or a browser binary, is read during init and then gone, so a restored session fetches it from the image again. For these cases, you can add a build hook, covered in “Working with hooks.” Figure 3 shows where it runs. Figure 3: Build and invoke with hooks Measure before you optimize Latency in an agentic application isn’t one number. A request spends time in AgentCore runtime getting a session ready to run your code, then in your code: model calls, tool calls, sub-agents, and streaming the response back. You fix these in different ways, so start by finding out which one dominates. AgentCore runtime publishes both as Amazon CloudWatch metrics in the AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore namespace. Latency is the time to first byte. OverheadLatency is the part that belongs to the platform, such as starting the microVM and restoring the snapshot on a new session. What you want How to get it TTFB (Time to first byte) Latency Runtime time OverheadLatency Your code’s time Latency − OverheadLatency Init time Measured in your code at startup (see the following example). items.title: OpenFold3 on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: Predict biomolecular structures
items.description: You can deploy OpenFold3-preview from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart . The OpenFold Consortium and the AlQuraishi Lab at Columbia University developed OpenFold3 as an open source biomolecular structure prediction model. With a few lines of code, you can typically deploy OpenFold3 into your own AWS account. You can then predict the 3D structures of proteins, DNA, RNA, small-molecule ligands, and the complexes they form. The endpoint runs with network isolation, which you can use to help keep your sequences within your AWS account. Computational drug discovery teams now use structure prediction as a core part of their work. Teams use it in target identification, antibody and protein engineering, and structure-based virtual screening. Teams have found running these models challenging. You need GPU infrastructure, a working CUDA and PyTorch stack, large model checkpoints, and a serving layer that handles requests that take minutes rather than milliseconds. SageMaker JumpStart can handle much of that work for you. OpenFold3 runs in an AWS-maintained container on a managed Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint. The endpoint is designed to handle request queuing and GPU warmup, and you can add autoscaling. In this post, we show you how to: Deploy OpenFold3-preview on a SageMaker asynchronous inference endpoint. Submit structure prediction jobs and interpret the results, including predicted structures and confidence scores. Run several predictions in parallel on multi-GPU instances . Supply your own multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) to improve prediction accuracy while helping keep your sequences private. Help reduce costs by scaling your endpoint to zero when it’s idle. Overview of OpenFold3 OpenFold3 is an all-atom structure prediction model. It predicts the joint 3D structure of a set of molecules from their sequences. It isn’t limited to single protein chains: It can fold multi-chain protein complexes, protein–nucleic acid assemblies, and protein–ligand complexes in one prediction. Attribute Details Developer OpenFold Consortium / AlQuraishi Lab, Columbia University Model type All-atom biomolecular structure prediction Inputs Protein, DNA, and RNA sequences. Small-molecule ligands as SMILES Outputs Predicted structures in mmCIF format, with confidence metrics (pLDDT, PAE, PDE) Version OpenFold3 0.4.1, of3-p2-155k checkpoint License Apache 2.0 JumpStart model ID huggingface-proteinfolding-openfold3 Supported instances ml.g6.2xlarge , ml.g6.4xlarge (default), ml.g6.12xlarge The OpenFold3 developers release its code and model weights under the Apache 2.0 license, and they publish the training data and methods. Research organizations and pharmaceutical companies can inspect the model, fine-tune it, and build on it under the terms of that license. The developers describe OpenFold3-preview as a research preview. Use cases Target and complex structure prediction – Predict structures for targets that have no experimental structure, including multi-chain assemblies and protein–nucleic acid complexes. Protein–ligand co-folding – Fold a protein together with a small molecule supplied as SMILES to generate binding-pose hypotheses for structure-based design. Antibody and protein engineering – Evaluate designed variants by predicting their structures and comparing confidence across candidates. High-throughput screening pipelines – Queue large batches of prediction jobs against an autoscaling endpoint and process the results directly from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). Why OpenFold3 uses asynchronous inference Most JumpStart models, such as large language models and embedding models, deploy to real-time endpoints. A real-time endpoint returns its response within a single request, and that request is capped at 60 seconds. Structure prediction works differently. Folding time grows with the number and length of the chains in a query, and real-world proteins and complexes often take several minutes. For this reason, OpenFold3 on JumpStart runs on SageMaker Asynchronous Inference : You upload the request to Amazon S3 and call InvokeEndpointAsync , which returns immediately. The endpoint queues the request and processes it, with an invocation timeout of up to 1 hour. The endpoint writes the result, or the error details, to an S3 location you choose. You can poll for it or get a notification through Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS). Two properties of asynchronous endpoints suit scientific workloads especially well. First, they queue bursts of requests internally, so you can submit a large batch of sequences without building your own job queue. Second, they can scale to zero instances when the queue is empty, which helps you avoid paying for idle instances between experiments. Prerequisites To follow this walkthrough, you need: An AWS account, and a SageMaker AI execution role for the endpoint. Following least privilege, this AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role needs read and write access only to the S3 prefix that you use for requests and results. For more information, see How to use SageMaker AI execution roles . IAM permissions for the identity that runs the code: to create, describe, invoke, and delete the model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint, plus iam:PassRole for the execution role. For the optional scale-to-zero section, it also needs AWS Application Auto Scaling and Amazon CloudWatch alarm permissions. In production, scope these permissions to your resources rather than using broad managed policies such as AmazonSageMakerFullAccess . For more information, see Complete the prerequisites for asynchronous inference. Access to Amazon SageMaker Studio , a SageMaker notebook instance, or a local IDE. The SageMaker Python SDK v3 and py3Dmol, which you can install with pip install "sagemaker>=3,<4" py3Dmol . Service quota for at least one ml.g6.4xlarge endpoint instance in your AWS Region. You also need quota for ml.g6.12xlarge if you follow the multi-GPU section. You can check you

items.title: FAA expands AI advice to manage air traffic congestion across entire US airspace
items.description: The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment. “After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10. items.title: Kitesurf is now open source
items.description: We introduced Kitesurf , our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to. That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers. A browser built for agents Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer. Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network. Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial announcement and how to use it in Browser Run’s developer documentation. What is inside the repository? Kitesurf builds on Cloudflare’s Developer Platform and APIs, alongside an ecosystem of open-source Rust packages compiled to WebAssembly: Blitz provides HTML parsing, the DOM, layout, and painting. Stylo provides CSS parsing, cascading, and computed styles. Boa runs JavaScript inside WebAssembly (as the last resort only when we can’t run JavaScript in Dynamic Workers). Linebender libraries provide text layout and 2D graphics, and Krilla generates PDF output. These projects made Kitesurf possible. They retain their respective licenses; the repository's NOTICE documents third-party notices. Kitesurf has three main parts: the Engine manages browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer draws the result. All packages, the engine, its Rust core, DOM shims, renderer, and Kitesurf CLI live separately in folders under the repository’s packages directory where you can explore how all the pieces fit together. Run your own Kitesurf To run Kitesurf locally, follow the repository's build requirements , then clone the repository , install dependencies, and start the engine: git clone https://github.com/cloudflare/kitesurf.git cd kitesurf pnpm install --frozen-lockfile pnpm run dev The first build compiles the Rust core and its dependencies, so give it some time. Subsequent builds reuse the build cache. Finally wrangler starts a local development server at http://127.0.0.1:8787 . Open that address to try a page in Chrome DevTools, or use it programmatically. You can use puppeteer with a NodeJS script: import puppeteer from "puppeteer-core"; const browser = await puppeteer.connect({ browserWSEndpoint: "ws://127.0.0.1:8787/devtools/browser", }); try { const page = await browser.newPage(); await page.goto("https://example.com/"); await page.screenshot({ path: "page.png" }); } finally { await browser.disconnect(); } Or you can point your AI harness at the local CDP port (agents love CDP) and watch it take full control of Kitesurf. Deploy to your Cloudflare account When you’re done changing and testing locally, you can deploy the engine to your own account and use Kitesurf from there instead of the Browser Run managed APIs we provide. Note that a Workers Paid plan is required because Kitesurf uses Dynamic Workers to create isolated Workers for pages. From the repository root: pnpm run deploy Help us make it better As with all of our open-sourced projects, Kitesurf lives in Github and we welcome forks and contributions . However, note that Kitesurf is under heavy development and we are focusing on making the engine more compatible (check out Web Platform Test evolution ), more reliable, and efficient . Focused fixes with tests, clear evidence, and a well-defined scope are much easier to review than large rewrites or unrelated cleanup, but all contribution does not have to be code: a small page that reproduces a rendering bug, a failing automation workflow, or a clear documentation correction can help us move forward. Stay tuned Kitesurf is evolving quickly. Stay tuned for updates in the blog and our changelog , and keep an eye on the official landing page for the latest on standards compatibility in Web Platform Tests page and benchmarks . items.title: Cost-optimizing AssemblyAI speech-to-text inference on AWS with Amazon EC2 Spot
items.description: Speech-to-text inference is computationally intensive. Each audio file triggers a pipeline of deep learning models (acoustic models, language models, and post-processing stages) running on NVIDIA GPUs to meet latency requirements. At scale, this means thousands of GPU instances running continuously. AssemblyAI needed a way to run GPU-intensive inference workloads cost-effectively at scale, without sacrificing the availability and latency guarantees their customers depend on. Running entirely on On-Demand Instances would be cost-prohibitive. Spot Instances offer significant savings, while Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) can reclaim them with a 2-minute warning when capacity is needed elsewhere. AssemblyAI needed an architecture that absorbs Spot interruptions gracefully while maintaining service level agreement (SLA) commitments. Additionally, customers in regulated industries, including healthcare, finance, and legal, must keep audio data within specific geographic boundaries. They implement strict data residency configurations in European AWS Regions. Available on AWS Marketplace , AssemblyAI provides an API for transcription, speaker detection, sentiment analysis, chapter detection, and personally identifiable information (PII) redaction. Their models transcribe and analyze speech for high-volume workloads across industries including technology, media, healthcare, and financial services. In this post, we show you how AssemblyAI runs cost-optimized AI inference at scale for their speech-to-text platform. The architecture uses Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) Spot Instances, and Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). Together, these services combine a flexible fleet of NVIDIA GPUs, ECS capacity providers, and a queue-based retry mechanism. The result is significant cost savings while maintaining SLA commitments across European AWS Regions. Solution overview AssemblyAI’s inference platform runs on Amazon ECS with compute capacity managed through ECS capacity providers. The fleet mixes Amazon EC2 Spot Instances and On-Demand Instances across multiple NVIDIA GPU instance families, running a single inference model per GPU at a scale of thousands of instances. The architecture is built on four pillars that work together to deliver cost-optimized and resilient inference: Amazon ECS capacity providers mixing Spot and On-Demand. Multi-family GPU Spot diversification across EC2 instance types (such as g4dn.xlarge, g4dn.2xlarge, g5.xlarge, g5.4xlarge, and g6.2xlarge). Queue-based retry architecture using Amazon SQS for interruption recovery. Regional deployment across US West (Oregon) us-west-2 and Europe (London) eu-west-2 for data residency compliance. The following diagram illustrates how this solution is deployed: Figure 1: AssemblyAI’s inference architecture on Amazon ECS with Amazon EC2 Spot GPU instances and an Amazon SQS-based retry mechanism An Amazon ECS cluster runs within a virtual private cloud (VPC) across multiple Availability Zones. The cluster hosts GPU-backed ECS tasks (shown as ECS Task, GPU Spot 1 and ECS Task GPU Spot 2) that poll the queue and process inference jobs. Each task retrieves audio files from Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and writes the completed transcription to a results store, which AssemblyAI configures to deliver the output to the end customer. When a Spot Instance receives an interruption notice, Amazon EventBridge invokes the Spot Interruption Handler (an AWS Lambda function). The handler returns the in-flight job to the Main Job SQS Queue so another healthy ECS task can pick it up. Customers configure their system to route jobs that exhaust retry attempts to a Dead Letter SQS Queue for investigation. Amazon CloudWatch Metrics monitors the health of the fleet and the Spot interruption events, providing observability across the system. Amazon ECS capacity providers and Spot diversification To optimize inference costs without compromising reliability, AssemblyAI configures multiple capacity providers in a single capacity provider strategy within each ECS cluster. An On-Demand capacity provider serves as an always-on baseline, and a Spot capacity provider spans different GPU instance families and Availability Zones to serve spikes of demand. Each capacity provider associates with an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group. Amazon ECS managed scaling automates the scaling of GPU instances based on the capacity provider weights and the pending inference tasks. When the task queue grows, the Spot capacity provider requests additional instances from the diversified pool. When demand drops, instances scale in gracefully. One of the most effective Spot best practices is to be flexible across a wide range of instance types to increase the chances of getting the aggregate compute capacity needed. Rather than depending on a single GPU instance family, AssemblyAI’s infrastructure spans three Amazon EC2 GPU instance families: g4dn instances – Powered by NVIDIA T4 GPUs, providing a cost-effective baseline for standard speech recognition models. g5 instances – Equipped with NVIDIA A10G GPUs, delivering higher throughput for more demanding model architectures. g6 instances – Featuring NVIDIA L4 GPUs, offering improved performance-per-dollar for larger models including large language model-based inference. By spreading demand across instance families and sizes, AssemblyAI draws from a significantly larger pool of available Spot capacity. Using the price-capacity optimized allocation strategy , Amazon EC2 provisions instances from the Spot capacity pools with the highest available capacity at the lowest price, reducing the likelihood of interruptions. Queue-based retry for interruption resilience Maintaining quality of service during Spot interruptions was a core design requirement. items.title: How Microcredentials Can Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI
items.description: Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics , governance , and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges. “AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance. Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union , the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology , and the International Organization for Standardization . The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias , security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap. Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies. Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust. Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance. The benefits of microcredentials Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program. Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment. For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles. Translating standards into microcredentials Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards , most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle. The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust. To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert .

items.title: Cost attribution and controls for AI developer and productivity tools on Amazon Bedrock
items.description: Amazon Bedrock provides built-in, zero-instrumentation cost attribution that traces every inference call back to the IAM principal that made it. The identity flows along with organizational tags, into AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0) and AWS Cost Explorer while keeping data inside the AWS security boundary. This post shows you how to use these capabilities to answer three questions that every FinOps and AI Platform leader asks as AI tool adoption scales: What is the real per-user cost? Which teams generate the most spend, and does that spend correlate with the value they deliver? How should next year’s budget scale with headcount and adoption? The approach works identically regardless of which AI coding or productivity tool makes the call. Claude Code, Claude Desktop, OpenAI Codex, ChatGPT Work, and OpenCode all invoke Amazon Bedrock through one of two inference endpoints: bedrock-runtime or bedrock-mantle , and Bedrock’s attribution mechanism operates at the endpoint layer, beneath any tool-specific logic. You configure identity propagation once, and every tool that routes inference through Bedrock inherits per-user cost visibility automatically. By the end of this post, you will have AWS IAM Identity Center configured with your external identity provider for per-user attribution, session tags (team, cost center) flowing into CUR 2.0, Amazon Athena queries and dashboard options for ongoing cost visibility, and a clear understanding of Bedrock-native usage controls to enforce spending limits. How Amazon Bedrock attribution works Amazon Bedrock records the IAM identity of every inference caller with no changes required to your API calls. When a user invokes a model through either the bedrock-runtime or bedrock-mantle endpoint, Bedrock captures the caller’s full IAM ARN, including the session name for federated users and publishes it to CUR 2.0 in the line_item_iam_principal column. In billing data, usage is aggregated per principal and per usage type for each export interval: one hour in an hourly export, one day in a daily export. CUR does not contain per-request cost. For per-prompt detail, use model invocation logs or request metadata tagging. Optionally, you can attach tags to IAM principals or pass session tags during federation to add organizational dimensions. These tags appear in CUR 2.0 with the iamPrincipal/ prefix and in Cost Explorer as filterable dimensions. The mechanism supports four access patterns: IAM users, per-application roles, federated identities, and large language model (LLM) gateways proxying to Bedrock. For a comparison of all four, see Introducing granular cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock . This post follows the federated identity pattern, which is the natural fit for AI coding and productivity tools where each developer or knowledge worker authenticates individually. Amazon Bedrock offers additional attribution mechanisms beyond IAM principal tracking that organizations can layer depending on their needs (see Appendix A for a comparison). With Application Inference Profiles, you can tag spend by workload on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. With Projects and Workspaces, you can isolate and tag spend on the bedrock-mantle endpoint. Per-request metadata tagging provides per-prompt token-level detail in model invocation logs for workloads that need granularity finer than finer than CUR 2.0’s per-usage-type aggregation per export interval. You can combine these, for example, IAM principal attribution for per-user dollars on your invoice alongside per-request metadata tags for per-prompt detail in logs. The choice depends on your goal (see Track usage and costs in Amazon Bedrock ). The attribution problem The developer and productivity tools run on each user’s machine and call Amazon Bedrock directly, or through an LLM gateway. Users authenticate by assuming a shared IAM role, so every API call appears as assumed-role/ / in billing. If every user assumes the role with the same fixed session name, or calls go through a gateway’s own role, CUR aggregates spend to a single principal. With IAM Identity Center, the session name is the user’s sign-in name, so each user gets their own principal. You can further enrich it with session tags (team, cost center, project). These fields flow into CUR 2.0’s line_item_iam_principal column and cost allocation tags with the iamPrincipal/ prefix, making per-user spend queryable alongside the dollars, with zero changes to your Bedrock API calls. Claude Platform on AWS and Claude for Enterprise route inference through Anthropic-managed infrastructure. For Claude Platform on AWS, usage is visible by workspace and API key in Anthropic’s admin console, and workspace tags flow to AWS billing. For Claude for Enterprise, per-user usage is visible in Anthropic’s admin console and Usage and Cost API. Spend limits are enforced natively by Anthropic. Prerequisites Before starting, make sure you have: An AWS account with IAM permissions to access Bedrock models you intend to use. AWS IAM Identity Center enabled in your management account. An external identity provider (Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, or Ping Identity) with SCIM provisioning capability. AWS CLI v2 configured on developer machines. AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR 2.0) enabled with IAM principal data and delivered to an S3 bucket. Cost allocation tags activated from the management (payer) account. An Athena table configured to query CUR 2.0 data (see the GitHub sample to get started). Step 1: Configure IAM Identity Center with your external IdP Configure your external identity provider as the identity source in AWS IAM Identity Center. Navigate to IAM Identity Center → Settings → Identity source → Change identity source. Select “External identity provider” and configure SAML 2.0 or SCIM connectivity with your IdP. Enable SCIM provisioning to automatically synchronize users and groups, including organizational attributes like team and department. Configure attribute m
