items.title: Run agents securely and efficiently with the next generation AgentCore runtime
items.description: AI agents have moved past one-off prompts. They now run multi-step workloads for hours at a time. The length of task that frontier agents can complete on their own doubles about every four months ( METR ), and 40 percent of large enterprises are scaling AI agents, up from 27 percent a year ago ( McKinsey ). As agents run longer and with more autonomy, the focus shifts from what agents can do to how securely, reliably, and economically they can operate at scale. Agents do more than traditional software: they execute code, navigate browsers, access sensitive data, and act on behalf of users. These capabilities introduce new security and infrastructure demands, making strong isolation essential for production deployments. Every agent session needs a secure, isolated environment. But delivering that isolation at scale introduces a fundamental challenge: balancing performance, cost, and efficiency. Pre-provisioned environments consume resources even when idle, driving up costs. On-demand environments reduce wasted capacity but introduce cold-start latency, delaying agent execution. Neither approach scales efficiently without trade-offs. As organizations move from deploying a handful of agents to running thousands of concurrent sessions, building and managing custom sandboxes becomes increasingly complex, expensive, and unpredictable. The challenge is evident. Only 15 percent of organizations have scaled orchestrated, multi-agent systems, and 70 percent say they can’t yet trust and govern their agents ( Deloitte ). Scaling agents shouldn’t mean choosing between security, speed, and cost. The next generation of agent infrastructure must deliver strong isolation with fast startup times, elastic scaling, and usage-based economics. Because as AI agents move into production, secure execution shouldn’t be the bottleneck. It should be the foundation that makes scale possible. The fastest path to production should also be the safest one. The next generation AgentCore runtime We built Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to help developers build, connect, and optimize agents securely at scale. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is the managed compute layer. It gives developers a fully managed environment to deploy and run agents without building or maintaining infrastructure. Since launching, our customers have been pushing their agents into increasingly complex workloads. As those workloads grow, so do the demands on the execution environment: more compute, more flexible billing, and trust boundaries that extend to data, not only compute. Agents reach production at scale if the infrastructure underneath was built for both scale and speed. Today we’re announcing updates to AgentCore runtime that meet those demands. The core guarantee stands: every session runs in its own hardware-isolated Firecracker micro virtual machine (MicroVM), with its own identity, policy, and audit trail. These updates expand what’s possible within that guarantee. Sessions now start up to 15x faster, scale to 4x more compute, and run up to 68% more efficiently, with the isolation boundary fully intact. Here’s what’s new. Run bigger workloads without waiting longer to start Teams building increasingly advanced agents asked for more flexibility: the ability to scale memory and compute within the isolated session to match the demands of their workloads. From large codebase compilations to browser-driven workflows to local model inference, the execution environment needs to keep pace. Sessions now scale 4x compared to the previous version, up to 8 vCPUs and 32 GB, with support for container images up to 10 GB. Sessions start in under 2 seconds, independent of image size and concurrency. You no longer need warm pools and pre-provisioned clusters to manage cold starts. “AgentCore Runtime lets us run AI-driven development at scale. Each coding agent session runs in its own hardware-isolated environment, which we need when agents execute code, and the runtime scales elastically with demand and starts fast every time, so our engineers move quickly without managing any infrastructure.” — Siwei Shen, VP of Engineering, Coinbase “Mission is using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime to power a natural-language query agent that helps users retrieve property and sales insights without navigating complex data systems. In our initial comparison of both runtime versions, the same workload delivered 35% faster cold starts for inference requests and 77% faster starts for health checks, while reducing measured runtime cost per call by 17%. The new AgentCore runtime gives us a compelling combination of faster agent experiences and more efficient resource utilization as we bring enterprise agents into production.” — Dr. Ryan Ries, Chief AI & Data Scientist, Mission Cloud “Our approach is to run Zuora’s cloud with automation and AI agents wherever we can, and that only works if the runtime is efficient and reliable. The next generation AgentCore runtime cut our memory footprint per invocation by around 60% in many use cases while handling more traffic at steady latency. That gives us a stronger cost profile as we expand agentic workloads across our platform.” — Brad Ruppert, VP of Cloud and Security, Zuora “The Rescale platform helps R&D and engineering teams accelerate product development with agentic digital engineering. Our engineering-specific agents validate simulation inputs, troubleshoot jobs, select hardware, and generate reports, while engineers stay in control. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime allows us to deploy and scale those agents in production without building or operating the underlying agent infrastructure, so we can deliver new agents to customers faster.” — Mark Whitney, VP Engineering, Rescale Stop paying for idle agents As teams move agents closer to production, they asked for billing that reflects how agents actually work. items.title: Migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base with your coding agent
items.description: With a customer-managed knowledge base on Amazon Bedrock , you provision and scale the vector store, tune the embedding model and index settings, and plan capacity for each new data source. The migration guide in the Agent Toolkit for AWS helps you migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base . Managed Knowledge Base takes over that work and adds new retrieval capabilities, and your team keeps control of the content and the application that uses it. Moving a production knowledge base means your team maps its configuration, creates the replacement, ingests content, updates the application’s retrieval call, and validates retrieval before switching traffic. To help, we added a knowledge base migration guide to the amazon-bedrock skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS . The guide gives your coding agent the context to plan the migration with you, starting with read-only discovery and a plan you review line by line. On your approval, the agent creates the new knowledge base and its data sources alongside the original, or writes a migrated infrastructure as code (IaC) template for your pipeline. Ingestion and updating your application’s Retrieve calls stay with you, and your agent can walk you through both. In this post, we explain why we recommend the move and how the migration guide works, review the prerequisites, install the skill, plan a migration, update the application’s retrieval call, and validate retrieval before cutover. Why move to Managed Knowledge Base We recommend Managed Knowledge Base because it balances ease of use, retrieval accuracy, and cost. AWS runs the store With a Managed Knowledge Base, Amazon Bedrock handles ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval, and the store scales automatically as your content grows. Hybrid search, which combines keyword and semantic matching, is always on, with no index to configure. The knowledge base includes a managed embedding model, a managed reranker, and a built-in parser for multimodal file types. You can still bring your own Amazon Bedrock embedding model when you create the knowledge base. On each retrieval request, you choose the managed reranker, an Amazon Bedrock reranking model, or no reranking. The managed reranker requires the managed embedding model. Built-in capabilities Managed Knowledge Base includes capabilities you’d otherwise build yourself: Native connectors ingest content directly from sources such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Microsoft SharePoint, and Atlassian Confluence. For the current list, see supported connectors . After the first full sync, later syncs pick up only changes, on demand or on a schedule. The Managed Knowledge Base includes a deletion safeguard to help protect against accidental bulk removal of indexed content. Access control list (ACL) awareness ingests document permissions with the content, so retrieval returns only what the signed-in user can access. For connectors that support it, such as Microsoft SharePoint and Atlassian Confluence, a real-time check against the source also catches permission changes since the last sync. ACL awareness doesn’t authenticate users, so your application must verify and pass the user’s identity. Agentic retrieval answers questions that a single search can’t by handling multi-part questions and retrieving iteratively. It can search more than one knowledge base in a single request. Integration with AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, exposes your knowledge base as a target. Any client that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) can then query the knowledge base, and the gateway handles authentication. Resource-based policies let applications in other AWS accounts use one team’s knowledge base. Scope each policy to the specific roles that call the knowledge base, and grant only the actions they use, such as bedrock:Retrieve . Agentic retrieval, AgentCore Gateway integration, and resource-based policies are not available on customer-managed knowledge bases. For the AWS Regions where managed knowledge bases are available, and the features that AWS GovCloud (US-West) doesn’t support, see Supported AWS Regions . Higher quotas As of this writing, higher default quotas change how you can organize content. With 200 data sources per knowledge base, you can group related content in one knowledge base. With 10,000 knowledge bases per account, per Region, each team or product line can use a separate knowledge base. Default quota Customer-managed Managed Knowledge bases per account, per Region 100 10,000 Data sources per knowledge base 5 200 Concurrent ingestion jobs per knowledge base 1 50 Query input characters 1,000 10,000 For current values, see Amazon Bedrock endpoints and quotas and Service quotas for managed knowledge bases . Pay for what you store and retrieve Cost is one of three things teams weigh when they consider this move, alongside customizability and direct control of the vector store. On a customer-managed knowledge base , you choose, provision, scale, and update the vector and text stores, and pay separately for the infrastructure you select. On a Managed Knowledge Base, those stages are part of the service, and storage and retrieval are metered directly. The pricing models can differ too. With a customer-managed knowledge base, storage and retrieval charges depend on the vector store you choose. Some stores charge for provisioned or minimum capacity, and others, such as Amazon S3 Vectors, a capability of Amazon S3, charge only for what you use. A Managed Knowledge Base is priced on what you store and retrieve, so cost follows real usage. Usage-based pricing can fit enterprise question-answering, policy, and support knowledge bases that run at low utilization. For current rates, see Amazon Bedrock pricing . For the parsers available on a customer-managed knowledge base and how each is billed, see Parsing options for your data source . items.title: Build composable, interoperable multi-agent systems with A2A on AWS
items.description: Agents in multi-agent systems that span organizational boundaries often need to collaborate in a composable, interoperable way, with agents that other organizations build and run. They need a way to discover each other, communicate, and exchange tasks without exposing internals or requiring the same framework on both sides. The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol addresses this constraint. Without A2A, building composable multi-agent systems across organizational boundaries requires custom integration code for each customer and framework. Independent software vendors (ISVs) can instead build composable, interoperable agents that work with the A2A-compatible frameworks their customers already use. While we frame this post around the ISV use case, the pattern also applies to organizations that expose agents across boundaries, whether to partners, customers, or internal teams that use different frameworks. As your system grows, you add skills by registering Agent Cards with the orchestrator, without changing the agents already running. In this post, we walk through a deployed reference architecture on AWS. A LangChain-based enterprise orchestrator communicates with a Strands Agents-based software as a service (SaaS) agent across organizational boundaries using A2A, with the enterprise and the SaaS provider in separate AWS accounts. Neither side depends on the other’s framework or SDK, and the two sides share no secrets. We cover the architecture and implementation patterns, then deploy the system from three Jupyter notebooks and run an end-to-end test. The A2A protocol is now a Linux Foundation project , and AWS is among the organizations that support it. With A2A, agents can discover each other, negotiate tasks, and collaborate across organizational boundaries through a standardized protocol. The protocol uses existing authentication standards such as OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC) for cross-boundary security, and is designed to work across A2A-compatible frameworks. In Open Protocols for Agent Interoperability Part 4: Inter-Agent Communication on A2A , we introduced A2A concepts and demonstrated two Strands agents communicating using the protocol on AWS. That post established the foundation with Agent Card discovery, structured task execution, and the A2A server pattern. This post builds on that foundation with cross-framework interoperability, cross-organizational trust boundaries, and OAuth in both directions. Solution overview Three agents run in two AWS accounts, one for the enterprise and one for the SaaS provider. The A2A protocol connects them, with OAuth authentication in both directions. Each account has its own Amazon Cognito user pool, so each side authenticates with its own identity provider. Figure 1: A2A agents across an enterprise account and a SaaS provider account During onboarding, the enterprise and the SaaS provider exchange only public values, such as identity provider URLs, client IDs, scopes, and endpoint URLs. Each side then trusts tokens from the other side’s user pool, and no secrets are shared. After onboarding, each request follows these steps: The enterprise app gets an access token from the enterprise’s Amazon Cognito user pool. The app sends a question over HTTPS to the user API in Amazon API Gateway, then polls for the answer. Amazon API Gateway forwards the request privately, through a VPC link and an internal Network Load Balancer, to the Enterprise Orchestrator, a LangChain agent. When its model decides that the question needs a compliance scan, the orchestrator gets its own token from the enterprise user pool, using a client secret stored in AWS Secrets Manager . The orchestrator sends an A2A request to the compliance SaaS agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, using the skill it read from the agent’s Agent Card at startup. The compliance agent checks the enterprise context agent’s Agent Card at the callback URL registered at onboarding, then gets a token from the SaaS provider’s own pool. The compliance agent calls back to the enterprise context agent for account metadata, finishes its scan, and returns the answer to the orchestrator and then to the app. On the enterprise side, two agents run on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate . The Enterprise Orchestrator is the entry point for users. LangChain provides the agent framework and tool-calling abstractions, and Amazon Bedrock provides the foundation models (FMs) that power each agent’s reasoning. The orchestrator uses LangChain and Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6). At startup, the orchestrator fetches the SaaS agent’s Agent Card from its well-known URL and creates a LangChain tool for each skill described on the card. The model then decides which tool to call based on the user’s question, so the orchestrator needs no hardcoded routing logic. It sends compliance scan requests over A2A with OAuth bearer tokens and summarizes the results for leadership. Users reach the orchestrator through an Amazon API Gateway HTTPS endpoint that accepts only tokens from the enterprise’s own pool. The second enterprise agent provides internal context. The Enterprise Context Agent is built with LangChain and Amazon Bedrock (Amazon Nova Lite). It provides internal account metadata such as internal policy rules, data classification, business criticality, and escalation contacts (team on-call rotations). The deployed agent uses the official a2a-sdk (AgentCard, AgentExecutor, and spec-conformant JSON-RPC routes), pinned to a2a-sdk[http-server]==1.2.2. The SaaS agent reaches the context agent through an API Gateway partner API that accepts only the SaaS provider’s callback token. Both enterprise agents run in private subnets of an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), with no public IP addresses. items.title: Fine-grained access control for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base tools
items.description: More enterprises are building AI agents into their daily work, and a common pattern is an agent that searches internal documents to compose its answers. A single organization might soon run hundreds of agents, each connected to many data sources and tools. This raises a question. When an agent searches on behalf of a user, can you make sure that it uses only the information that user is allowed to see? Consider AnyCompany, a fictional company that builds an internal assistant shared by all employees. An employee in department A asks, “Compare my department’s business plan with the notice to all departments, and list the initiatives that are behind schedule.” The agent writes its own search queries and keeps searching internal documents until it has enough information. Employees in department B ask the same assistant the same question. If the application doesn’t scope searches to each user, the department B business plan can end up in an answer to an employee in department A. If you replace the departments with customer companies, the same problem occurs in a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) architecture where multiple customers share one assistant and knowledge base. Controlling access to multi-tenant data through this agent is harder than in traditional applications. In a traditional application, the application code determines who the signed-in user is and searches with that user’s permissions. In an agent, a large language model (LLM) decides at runtime which tool to call and with which arguments. If a search tool takes “who to search as” as an argument, the LLM decides that value too. A prompt injection or an LLM error might then make the agent search as a different employee. In this post, we build an internal assistant for AnyCompany. All employees share the same agent and knowledge base, yet each employee can search only the documents they’re allowed to view. We use Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base as the search backend and expose it to the agent as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The design principle is to not let the LLM decide who the user is. Instead, trusted code decides, based on information that your identity provider has verified. On top of that, we add independent layers of defense in case that mechanism has a bug or is bypassed. Solution overview Managed Knowledge Base has a feature called ACL awareness . When a search request includes a user context ( userContext ) with the user’s email in userId , the knowledge base returns only the documents that user is allowed to view. If your application calls the search API directly, the application code sets the search scope from the authentication result. Build multi-tenant agentic chat applications on enterprise data with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base shows this pattern. When you expose the knowledge base as an MCP tool through AgentCore Gateway, however, userContext becomes a tool argument, and the LLM constructs its value. Neither the gateway nor the knowledge base verifies that this value belongs to the authenticated user. This solution injects verified user attributes into tool calls at the tool layer (AgentCore Gateway). It then scopes the search by those attributes at the resource layer (Managed Knowledge Base). The sample stores three documents in a single knowledge base: business plans for department A and department B, and a notice shared with all departments. Two users, user-a in department A and user-b in department B, search through the same agent. The following diagram shows the architecture. Figure 1: Solution architecture The request flow is as follows. The step numbers correspond to the numbers in Figure 1. Figure 1 omits the call from the web app to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, so its step numbers differ from the diagram in the repository README . The user signs in with Amazon Cognito and receives an access token, a JSON Web Token (JWT). A pre token generation AWS Lambda trigger adds an email claim to it. The agent forwards this token in the Authorization header when it sends MCP requests to the gateway. The JWT authorizer of the gateway validates the signature, expiration, and client ID of the token. A request interceptor (an AWS Lambda function) on the gateway resolves the email from the validated token and overwrites the userContext argument of tools/call . Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (Policy in AgentCore) evaluates the modified request against a Cedar policy. It denies the request if userContext.userId doesn’t match the email claim in the JWT. The connector target calls the Managed Knowledge Base search API with the execution role of the gateway. The resource-based policy of the knowledge base denies searches from principals other than this role. With ACL awareness, the knowledge base returns only chunks from documents that the userContext user is allowed to view. The four mechanisms map to layers and lines of defense as follows. Tool layer (AgentCore Gateway) Resource layer (Managed Knowledge Base) Primary defense Request interceptor: injects userContext deterministically from the verified token, which helps prevent the LLM or the client from spoofing it ACL awareness: returns only the documents that the userContext user is allowed to view Secondary defense Policy in AgentCore: checks the injected userContext against the token and denies requests that don’t match Resource-based policy: denies search requests from principals other than the gateway execution role For requests that go through the gateway, the two primary defenses are enough to achieve fine-grained access control, as long as no other principal can call the knowledge base. ACL awareness filters results based on the userContext that it receives and isn’t an authorization mechanism by itself . items.title: From prototype to production: Engineering agents with Agent DLC
items.description: Over the past year, AI agents have moved from exploration into engineering. Enterprise teams are shipping large language model (LLM) systems that call tools, orchestrate APIs, and answer questions over internal knowledge. A successful demo can show what an agent is capable of. Before release, the team needs to answer a further question: “ Is this agent ready for production? ” The person responsible for that decision needs evidence that the agent meets the agreed requirements. To make that decision consistently, teams need a repeatable, affordable way to assess the agent’s current behavior and whether the latest change has improved it. In traditional software development, teams answer these questions with unit tests, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD), and passing builds. Those mechanisms are necessary but not sufficient for agents, for three reasons, each requiring additional checks. This post explains these three properties and presents a measured case where an aggregate metric hides a coverage problem. It then introduces the Agent Development Lifecycle (Agent DLC): one lifecycle, two loops, and a single explicit standard for judging every change. A note on terminology: Throughout this post, gold standard means one specific artifact: the bundle of verifiable criteria, their thresholds, and the approved examples they are checked against. Business owners approve this standard as the basis for acceptance decisions. 1. Three properties of agents that require additional engineering practices Conventional software testing and CI/CD still apply to agents, but three properties require additional checks. First, agents are non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different outputs and execution paths. Second, changes to prompts, tool descriptions, retrieval settings, or memory configuration can alter behavior in ways that a text review alone can’t reveal. Third, model endpoints, knowledge bases, and external APIs can change independently of the repository and affect agent behavior. Table 1 summarizes the engineering practices needed to address each property. Table 1. What each property invalidates, and what it requires instead. Property The conventional answer Why it falls short What Agent DLC requires Non-determinism One assertion per case in CI Measures a single sample of a distribution. Passes and fails for reasons unrelated to your change Run each example k times. Judge on pass rate and failure distribution Prompts are source code Review the diff, approve the change Behavior can’t be read off the text of a prompt Every prompt, tool, retrieval, and memory change is versioned with an evaluation attached, and the lineage is kept Dependencies move on their own Pin versions, validate on upgrade Doesn’t fire because nothing in your repository changed Re-run the standard on a schedule and alert on deviations from the baseline 2. A measured example: High retrieval precision can hide missing information The following example shows how the choice of metrics affects diagnosis. We built a reference implementation to exercise the method end to end: an internal policy assistant answering HR policy questions over a document knowledge base. We chose a narrow, well-scoped domain to make the evaluation and diagnosis straightforward to follow. The following results were measured on this reference implementation. It isn’t a customer outcome and it isn’t a benchmark result. The accompanying AWS Samples repository includes infrastructure deployment, the HR agent, custom evaluators, and scripts for baseline evaluation and prompt-change re-evaluation ( 09-run-eval.sh and 10-optimize-prompt.sh ). It also includes optional checks for judge repeatability, model comparison, cost, and latency. The scripts reproduce the workflow. Scores can vary across runs and repository versions. Three golden questions, five measures each: Groundedness : Decompose the answer into claims and check each against the retrieved sources. Chunk-level source precision : Is each retrieved chunk, as a whole, necessary for this question? Fact-level source precision : Decompose each chunk into individual facts and check whether each fact is necessary. Retrieval coverage : For each sub-question, does any retrieved chunk answer it? Response precision : Of the claims in the answer, how many are necessary? Table 2. First evaluation round. Measured on the reference implementation. Not a customer outcome. Question Groundedness Chunk-level precision Fact-level precision Retrieval coverage Verdict Performance review 0.83 1.00 0.59 1.00 Pass Benefits enrollment 0.90 1.00 0.53 1.00 Pass Sick-leave certificate 0.39 1.00 0.09 0.00 Fail Chunk-level precision is 1.00 for all three questions. A release gate based only on this metric would accept all three answers. Fact-level precision tells a different story: 0.59, 0.53, 0.09. For the third question, roughly nine out of ten facts in the retrieved material are irrelevant to what was asked. Chunk-level precision only asks whether a passage is on topic. It doesn’t measure how much of the passage is relevant. Then we changed exactly one thing: the system prompt. We added three constraints: ground strictly in retrieved content, ignore irrelevant retrieved content, and keep answers focused. The agent, the knowledge base, the evaluators, and the questions were untouched, so the before-and-after differs by one variable. Table 3. After a prompt-only change. One change, two opposite outcomes. Performance review, before Performance review, after Sick leave, before Sick leave, after Groundedness 0.83 0.87 0.39 (fail) 0.31 (still fail) Fact-level precision 0.59 0.85 0.09 0.04 Response precision 0.58 0.73 0.33 — The first question improved substantially. The third got worse. The evaluation suggested where to investigate before we made the change. items.title: Google pushes privacy angle as Gemini-powered smartglasses debut starting at $395
items.description: Smartglasses have always faced an uphill road to acceptance. Not only is propping a computer up on your nose an uncomfortable proposition, but the privacy aspect has been vexing people since the Google Glass days . Now, Google is ready to take another swing at " intelligent eyewear " for the Gemini era after previewing its plans a couple of times. The first glasses are up for preorder today from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, but they're no impulse buy. These devices are a collaboration between Google, Samsung, and the aforementioned eyewear designers. Gentle Monster and Warby Parker have each designed a few different frames, with options for transparent and tinted lenses. Samsung is providing the computing hardware that fits inside them, and Google has the software covered. Warby Parker has designed three frames for Google eyewear, called Alden, Reid, and Wren (see above). They are available with both standard optical and sun lenses in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black colors at $395 and higher. Warby Parker is only selling devices in the US. Gentle Monster has gone a bit further with six styles, but Google hasn't told us any names for those yet. They come in dark red, pink, gray, and yellow colors and are available with clear, tinted, blue, or brown lenses. The Gentle Monster styles start a little higher at $449, and they will be available in the US and South Korea. Read full article Comments

items.title: Build autonomous AI agents with Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI
items.description: Java teams have established JVM tooling, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, and operational patterns, yet taking AI agents from prototype to production is hard: agent frameworks do not solve scalability, governance, security, and operational concerns by default. Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI close those gaps, so Java teams can build autonomous AI agents that plan, call tools and APIs, and maintain context across multi-turn conversations. Agentic AI is moving beyond prompt-response interactions toward autonomous systems that execute complex multi-step tasks. Java remains one of the widely used programming languages in enterprise software. Teams have existing CI/CD pipelines, operational expertise, and established patterns built around the JVM. Spring AI brings AI capabilities to the JVM through familiar Spring patterns: auto-configuration, dependency injection, and composable advisors. Developers can build AI agents using the same idioms they use for REST APIs, security, and data access. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. With AgentCore, you can build, deploy, and operate AI agents at scale. It is framework-agnostic and model-agnostic: you bring your preferred agent framework and foundation model (FM). With AgentCore, you can access the production infrastructure you need: managed runtime, memory, browser automation, code execution, and identity management. In this post, we show you how to build autonomous AI agents in Java using Spring AI and Amazon Bedrock with spring-ai-agentcore . We explore the key implementation patterns for two systems. The first is a single-agent travel assistant that demonstrates tool calling and memory. The second is a multi-agent intelligent document processing (IDP) system that shows how specialist agents, a rules engine, and alerting work together. Prerequisites To follow along with this walkthrough, you need the following: Java – JDK 21 (required) Spring Boot – 4.1 (with Spring AI 2.0 and spring-ai-agentcore 2.0) Maven – 3.9+. Node.js – 18+ (for the React frontend) Terraform – 1.5+. Docker – with Buildx for multi-architecture builds. AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) – v2, configured with credentials. An AWS account . What makes a system an agent A chat completion call can generate text, but it can’t decide what to do next, reach into external systems, or remember what happened yesterday. An agent can, because it unites three capabilities: Planning – Given a goal, the model breaks it into steps, prioritizes them, and revises the plan as new information arrives. Tool use – Beyond generating text, the model can select and invoke external functions such as APIs, databases, and code interpreters to act in the world. Memory – Context carries across turns (short-term) and across sessions (long-term), so each decision builds on what came before. A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application has limited tool use (retrieval) but no planning loop. An agent has all three, operating in a goal-directed loop until the task is complete or it determines it cannot proceed. The following diagram shows these capabilities in an end-to-end agentic pipeline, from request to grounded answer. Figure 1: Agentic reference architecture. A request flows through the runtime, guardrails, classification, a specialist agent, tools, the foundation model, memory, rules, and human review to a grounded answer, with resilience and observability as cross-cutting concerns The pipeline has 11 stages. A client submits a document and question. The request passes through a runtime gateway for authentication and rate limiting, then input guardrails screen for harmful content. A router classifies the document and routes it to a specialist agent, which plans its workflow and calls tools, the Amazon Bedrock foundation model, memory, and a rules engine as needed. Low-confidence or flagged results go to a human review queue before the grounded answer returns to the client. Resilience, observability, logging, and least-privilege AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) apply across all stages. Solution overview The solution consists of two deployable systems that share common patterns: Travel agent – A single autonomous agent with tool calling (weather lookups, itinerary search), streaming responses, conversation memory, and resilience patterns. This is the recommended starting point. IDP multi-agent system – A multi-agent intelligent document processing platform with five specialist agents (Lawyer, Mortgage, Insurance, Tax, General), rules and workflow engine, alerting, and observability. This demonstrates production patterns at a scale. Both systems share the following architecture: Spring Boot application with Spring AI ChatClient, Spring AI agentcore and Amazon Bedrock Converse API. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, defines the contract (POST /invocations , GET /ping ) for managed deployment. Conversation memory through AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for both short-term and long-term context. Tool calling with @Tool annotated methods. Structured output mapped to Java records. ARM64 container image optimized for AWS Graviton. Modular Terraform for infrastructure provisioning. The travel assistant is the recommended starting point. The following diagram illustrates how a Spring Boot agent interacts with AgentCore runtime, tools, memory, and models available on Amazon Bedrock. Figure 2: Single-agent travel assistant. The Spring Boot application exposes both REST endpoints for the React UI and the AgentCore runtime contract, calling Amazon Bedrock through the Converse API while tool calling, streaming, and memory run inside one code base. The travel assistant runs a single Spring Boot application with two entry points, the /invocations and /ping contract required by AgentCore runtime. items.description: Language model (LM) alignment improves model outputs to reflect human preferences while preserving the capabilities of the base model. The most common alignment approaches are (i) reinforcement learning, which maximizes the expected reward under a KL-divergence constraint, and (ii) best-of-NNN alignment, which selects the highest-reward output among NNN independent samples. Despite their widespread use, the fundamental limits of reward improvement under a KL budget remain poorly understood. items.title: OpenAI Codex on Amazon Bedrock
items.description: Developers increasingly use Codex with Amazon Bedrock to explore unfamiliar code, make changes, and handle repetitive engineering work. For platform teams, the challenge is to make those tools available without creating a second model-access, identity, and operations stack. Codex can use Amazon Bedrock for inference with supported OpenAI models. In this post, we show how to fit that path into the AWS identity, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), Regional, and observability practices your organization already uses. Codex still runs on the developer workstation. The main design choice is how its model requests reach Amazon Bedrock and where your organization applies policy and operational controls. We begin with a small, least-privilege pilot and work through the checks that matter before access expands. The examples use GPT-5.6 Sol. Before starting the pilot, review Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock to confirm that Sol, Terra, or Luna is available in the AWS Region and inference path you plan to use. Recommended default: Start with Native AWS Access for a small, least-privilege pilot. Choose AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, when you want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for routing or Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Choose an LLM Gateway when a platform team wants to enforce controls in the request path. A custom integration is the advanced version of the LLM Gateway pattern, not a quick start. The examples come from the open source Guidance for Codex on AWS repository. It includes quick starts for Native AWS Access, AgentCore Gateway, LiteLLM on ECS, Portkey, the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT), and the Amazon CloudWatch setup used later in the post. Choose the quick start that matches your architecture, use it for the pilot, and adapt it to your environment. Choose your rollout path Authentication is only one part of an enterprise rollout. Decide who can use the service and which models and Regions are approved. Also define where configuration lives, what telemetry to collect, how usage is allocated, and which skills or Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers are allowed. The following table maps those needs to an access path and an owning team. Choose the access path that provides the controls you need now. The most straightforward path that meets the requirement usually has the lowest operational overhead. Decision rules Native AWS Access is the usual starting point when AWS identity and IAM controls are enough for the pilot. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Within the platform, AgentCore Gateway fits teams that want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for routing, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, or related controls. A large language model (LLM) Gateway fits organizations that already operate a gateway or want to enforce controls in the request path. Building a custom gateway is the advanced version of this option. The following diagram compares where identity, routing, policy, telemetry, and operational ownership sit across the three rollout paths. Figure 1: Codex runs on the developer workstation in each scenario. Native AWS Access uses AWS IAM Identity Center, a configured AgentCore Gateway can apply managed routing and Guardrails, and a configured LLM Gateway can apply request-path controls Native AWS Access If Native AWS Access fits the pilot, the repository’s Native AWS Access quick start provides the complete procedure and supporting files. The following abbreviated walkthrough focuses on the sequence and the checks that matter most. Use your workforce identity provider for sign-in Employees continue to sign in through the identity provider they already use. In this example, Okta handles authentication through Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) and provisions users and groups into IAM Identity Center through System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM). IAM Identity Center then issues the temporary AWS credentials used by Codex. The identity provider is not configured in Codex. Prerequisites Add each pilot user to a dedicated group in the workforce identity system and provision that group to IAM Identity Center. Keep the assignment limited to the pilot. Choose an Amazon Bedrock Region and an OpenAI model available to the pilot identity, plus an inference profile if the selected API requires one. Check Sol, Terra, and Luna separately for the chosen account, Region, and inference path. Grant only the Amazon Bedrock model inference permissions used by Codex, any direct validation commands, and the selected observability destination. Prepare a non-production repository and name a rollback owner. Configure The pilot has three checks. First, sign in using the IAM Identity Center profile configured for the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and call Amazon Bedrock Runtime directly. Next, point Codex to the approved model. Finally, run a safe Codex task. The direct call isolates AWS access problems. The final step confirms the Codex configuration. Step 1: Sign in and validate Amazon Bedrock Runtime access. aws sso login --profile codex-bedrock export AWS_PROFILE=codex-bedrock aws bedrock-runtime converse --model-id us.openai.gpt-5.6-sol --messages '[{"role":"user","content":[{"text":"Reply with OK"}]}]' --region us-east-2 This command creates a short-lived AWS session and checks whether the profile can invoke the chosen model in the chosen Region. If it fails, resolve the profile, Region, model or inference-profile access, or IAM permissions before configuring Codex. Step 2: Configure the Codex provider. # ~/.codex/config.toml (or managed user configuration) model_provider = "amazon-bedrock" model = "openai.gpt-5.6-sol" [model_providers.amazon-bedrock.aws] profile = "codex-bedrock" region = "us-east-2" The model value is the Codex model ID. The profile selects the AWS IAM Identity Center session, and region tells Codex which AWS Region to use. Keep

items.title: Semantic diffing of formal policies with anti-unification
items.description: When reviewing code, you start with a diff. You wouldn’t compare two 3,000-line files by eye and hope to spot every change. Formal policies can be even harder to compare because a textual diff often highlights syntactic changes that don’t affect meaning. Reorder two conjuncts, swap the arguments of an equality, or use an equivalent predicate, and much of the file might appear changed. A real change in behavior, such as an Or where the requirement says and , can get lost in that noise. A semantic diff shows what two policies have in common and where they disagree. The open source engine used in this post computes this diff using anti-unification , which finds a most specific common pattern for two expressions. Plotkin’s 1970 paper gives the classical formulation. The engine works over an e-graph, which keeps track of expressions known to be equal. We supply the algebraic laws and domain rules that justify those equalities, such as equating an external destination with one that isn’t internal. The result shows the shared parts once and keeps both versions of each differing part for review. If no differences remain, the policies are equivalent under those laws and rules. When the rules or the search are incomplete, a remaining difference might reflect an equivalence the engine has not found. One use case is autoformalization. Autoformalization translates natural language into a formal language. Suppose you want to turn requirements into SMT-LIB , the standard input language for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers such as Z3 and cvc5, or into Cedar or Dogwood to control authorization in your software system. A large language model (LLM) generates the formal artifact from the prose. The model writes the artifact. It plays no part in computing the diff. Run the model twice, and it might produce two different formalizations, with no ground truth to identify the correct one. A semantic diff shows where they agree and where they differ. Generate more candidates by varying the model, prompt, or sampling temperature. Comparing them shows which parts stay the same and which vary. Review the varying parts first. Requirements can also become OpenShell sandbox policies or Common Expression Language (CEL) expressions. OpenShell uses YAML to describe an agent’s filesystem and network access. CEL is embedded in applications to evaluate expressions, including policy conditions. These languages and formats differ in what they express, but translations into any of them can disagree about a condition, a scope, or an event. The following table gives illustrative disagreements: Language or format Policy focus Example disagreement Cedar Who can perform an action on a resource, under which conditions. One translation requires ownership and approval. Another accepts either. Dogwood Authorization involving the current request and recent event history. One translation checks a successful prior response. Another checks a request event. OpenShell policies An agent’s filesystem and network access, including rules for particular binaries. One translation permits repository-scoped GET . Another permits organization-scoped POST . CEL Conditions evaluated over inputs supplied by a host application. One translation requires production for both allowed ports. Another requires it for only one. In each worked example, we compare translations of the same requirement within one policy context. We encode the relevant syntax as terms and declare the equalities used in the comparison. The engine reads these encodings. It doesn’t import native policies from the four formats. The idea is a formal-methods analogue of semantic entropy , described by Farquhar et al. in Nature (2024). That approach samples several natural-language answers, clusters those that entail one another, and reports a single number. For formal outputs, anti-unification preserves more information. It identifies the shared structure and each divergence instead of returning only a score. Counterexamples help explain the consequences of a disagreement. An SMT solver can find a concrete assignment that satisfies one formula and violates the other. A reviewer can then trace that assignment through the formulas to understand the conflicting decisions. The anti-unifier gives a different view: it organizes the shared structure and the fragments that differ, without issuing an SMT query. A solver or policy validator can help resolve those fragments. We assume you can read S-expression syntax, as in SMT-LIB, and know what an authorization policy is. E-graphs and anti-unification are explained as they come up. When several translations agree on part of a requirement, the diff shows that part once. Where they disagree, it keeps the alternatives visible for review. How semantic diffing represents disagreement Say a policy-generation pipeline hands you two candidate rules for this requirement: sensitive data sent to an external destination must be encrypted . Rule A Rule B sensitive ( data ) ∧ external ( dst ) → encrypted ¬ internal ( dst ) ∧ sensitive ( data ) → audited Whether these are the same rule isn’t obvious. The conditions are reordered, external is expressed indirectly as not internal , and the conclusions do not match. The engine computes a most specific anti-unifier for these terms. In its input language, the two rules are S-expressions. items.title: Detecting and recovering from silent data corruption on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
items.description: Silent data corruption (SDC) happens when hardware, such as a GPU, returns a wrong but plausible number and raises no error. In distributed training, the wrong number can flow into the gradients and weights of every replica. Loss can still look normal for hours, and by the time a team notices an unexplained divergence or a weaker model, the compute is spent. It happens at scale: during a 54-day period of Llama 3 405B pre-training on up to 16K H100 GPUs, Meta attributed 6 of 419 unexpected job interruptions to silent data corruption, and those were only the cases that interrupted the job and were traced to SDC. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod already replaces nodes that report a fault: the health-monitoring agent watches for GPU errors, deep health checks stress-test nodes, and automatic node recovery swaps out bad hardware. SDC slips past all of these features, because the hardware never reports anything. Detection has to come from the training job itself. In this post, we add three checks to a PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP) training loop to detect SDC. When a check fires, we map the suspect rank to its node, contain the corruption, and have SageMaker HyperPod replace the node. Each check covers a different place where a fault can land: A non-finite gradient check catches NaN, Inf, and overflow in a GPU’s forward or backward pass, on the step it happens, and NaN or Inf that the gradient all-reduce introduces. A ring replay audit catches finite wrong values. On audit steps, every GPU recomputes a micro-batch from another node and compares the loss bit for bit and the gradients by fingerprint. A weight fingerprint comparison catches corruption in the optimizer step and in stored weights, by comparing every replica’s weights after the update. We tested the checks with software-injected faults on a SageMaker HyperPod cluster with 4 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs), and repeated every test on three instances, the minimum the checks need. The full code of this solution is available in the accompanying GitHub repository . How silent data corruption happens and why the usual checks miss it SDC comes from manufacturing defects (marginal transistors that slip past vendor screening) and silicon aging in a specific compute unit, most often a multiply-accumulate lane in a tensor core, which is exactly the hardware model training hammers. That marginal circuit computes correctly most of the time and wrong only under stress: high temperature, voltage droop, or specific operand patterns. Because the arithmetic logic path has no ECC or parity (unlike memory), the wrong result, say 4.0001 instead of 4.0000, is never flagged, and it flows through activations and gradients into every replica’s weights. The reason it is so hard to catch is that SDC is in the compute path, and every integrity check you already have guards a different boundary : Check What it guards Why it misses SDC ECC memory Catches bit flips in memory, not wrong math. There is no ECC on a tensor-core result. Xid errors (NVRM) GPU driver/hardware faults The GPU raises an Xid when it detects a fault. SDC by definition raises none, so nothing lands in /aws/sagemaker/Clusters/ HMA logs. DCGM deep health check hardware faults Misses defects that need your workload’s operands, thermal state, or timing. Runs on an idle node, outside your job. NVLink / PCIe / EFA checksums transport Verify bytes arrived as sent, not that they were computed correctly. Checkpoint checksums storage round-trip A poisoned-but-consistent checkpoint checksums fine. The way to catch SDC is to check the result of the computation itself. Solution overview The loop has four steps. Your training job does the first two, and the last two use Kubernetes and SageMaker HyperPod features: Step 1. Detect: Three checks in your training loop name a suspect GPU by comparing data-parallel replicas. Step 2. Localize: On SageMaker HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), the Kubernetes node name contains the instance ID, so mapping a suspect rank to a node is a lookup. Step 3. Contain and correlate: Stop the job, cordon the node, and look at its GPU metrics in the SageMaker HyperPod observability dashboards. Step 4. Confirm and recover: Confirm when the alarm is ambiguous, replace the node after review, and resume from a checkpoint saved before the suspect window. Figure 1: A SageMaker HyperPod EKS cluster with three p5 nodes running training pods and SDC checks. Node 1 raises an alarm for rank 13, and the proposed steps cordon the node, check GPU metrics, replace it, and restart training It helps to see the loop as layers, each adding something different: Layer Source What it adds Catches truly silent SDC? 1. Non-finite gradient check Your training script Names a GPU whose local gradient is NaN or Inf, before the all-reduce, and stops the step if the reduced gradient is NaN or Inf Only faults that become NaN, Inf, or overflow 2. Ring replay audit Your training script Every GPU recomputes another node’s micro-batch and compares the loss bits and gradient fingerprints Yes, for finite compute-path faults that change the loss or a gradient, on audit steps 3. Weight fingerprint comparison Your training script Names a replica whose weights differ from a strict majority after the update Yes, for optimizer-step and stored-weight faults on one copy. Blind to compute-path faults and to sharded weights 4. Localization Your training script, using SageMaker HyperPod node names Maps a suspect rank to an instance ID from the Kubernetes node name n/a: it localizes 5. DCGM correlation HyperPod observability add-on The suspect GPU’s DCGM metrics around the alarm It confirms faults only where they also appear in hardware counters. Clean telemetry doesn’t clear a node. 6. Deep health check StartClusterHealthCheck (DCGM L4) An on-demand hardware diagnostic on the suspect node It catches hardware defects its own test patterns trigger. Triage, not proof 7

items.title: Introducing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: AI agents and applications that answer questions about recent events, product releases, prices, or regulations need information newer than their model’s training data. Until now, Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore delivered that information to agents through AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. That means creating a gateway and a web search target and calling the tool from an MCP client. The setup fits platform teams that share one search policy across many agents, but it’s more than you need when your own code only requires search results. Today, we’re announcing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With it, your own code can search the web with a single API call. It returns ranked results from a web index that Amazon operates, each with a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time. You call it from the AWS SDKs or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), signed with the same AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) credentials you use for your other AWS services. There are no resources to create first. Authenticate, call, and get results. Use it in an application, an agent loop you write yourself, or a data pipeline. Why a standalone API? The AgentCore Gateway is the recommended path for most agentic workloads. It gives agents one secure Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that combines web search with your other tools. It also handles inbound and outbound authentication, semantic tool selection, and optional MCP sessions . But developers told us they also need a lower-level integration point for scenarios where the gateway is not the right fit: Custom orchestration frameworks – Developers building their own agent loops, or using frameworks like LangChain or LlamaIndex, want to call web search directly as a tool within their orchestration logic rather than routing through a gateway. Non-agent use cases – Not every application that needs web grounding is an agent. Search-powered dashboards, fact-checking pipelines, content enrichment workflows, and monitoring systems all benefit from real-time web results without requiring agent infrastructure. Tighter control over the request lifecycle – Some developers want to manage retries, caching, and error handling themselves rather than delegating to the gateway. Simpler integration for existing applications – Applications that already have their own API layer can call the Web Search API directly, adding web grounding without adopting the full AgentCore Gateway stack. The Web Search API complements the gateway. It runs on the same search infrastructure that powers Alexa+, Kiro, Quick, and other Amazon products, with the same quality and compliance posture, exposed as a direct API operation. How it works The Web Search API is the InvokeWebSearch operation on the bedrock-agentcore data plane, the same endpoint that other AgentCore tools such as AgentCore Browser , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, use. Requests are signed with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) from your standard AWS credentials, so there’s no API key or secret to manage. Figure 1: How a Web Search API request flows The numbered steps are: Your application calls InvokeWebSearch with the AWS SDKs or the AWS CLI, which sign the request with SigV4 using its AWS credentials. From a virtual private cloud (VPC), the call can go through an interface VPC endpoint. The API checks with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) that the caller has bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch on the AWS managed web search tool. The API applies the filters in the request: the domains to include or exclude and the publication time range. The API searches a web index that Amazon operates. Queries are served inside AWS and aren’t sent to a third-party search engine. The API returns up to maxResults ranked results, each with a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time. The calling identity needs one IAM permission on an AWS managed resource. It’s the same action and resource that a gateway’s service role uses for web search, so one policy covers both routes. For details, see Grant permission to call the API . { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "InvokeWebSearch", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch", "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-west-2:aws:tool/web-search.v1" } ] } A first search request The following example searches two trusted domains for pages published in 2026, in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2), with the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) : import boto3 client = boto3.client("bedrock-agentcore", region_name="us-west-2") response = client.invoke_web_search( webSearchId="web-search.v1", searchQuery="multi-region EKS cluster deployment best practices", maxResults=10, filters={ "domainFilter": {"include": ["aws.amazon.com", "kubernetes.io"]}, "publishedDateFilter": {"publishedAfter": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"}, }, ) for result in response["results"]: print(result.get("publishedAt"), result.get("title"), result.get("url")) Every result has a text extract. The title, URL, and publication date come back when the index has them, so read them with get . One result from a live call, shortened: { "title": "One Amazon EKS, many edges: How to choose your edge container strategy on AWS", "url": "https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/containers/one-amazon-eks-many-edges-how-to-choose-your-edge-container-strategy-on-aws/", "text": "Separate the standard from the deployment model Choosing the wrong platform isn't really the issue. ...", "publishedAt": "2026-09-25T15:52:00Z" } That’s the full integration. items.title: ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in October 2026
items.description: At AWS, we believe AI builders should be able to choose the right model for every task, trust their agents in production, and see clearly what their AI workloads cost. That belief guides how we invest across our portfolio. Amazon Bedrock gives you access to leading models and the tools to build and scale AI applications securely. We extend this foundation with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , which provides the platform to build, connect, and optimize agents using any model and any framework. That includes Strands , our open source agent development toolkit. Together, they take you from first prototype to production. As agents move into core business workflows, the bar rises. You need the flexibility to use different models as tasks, budgets, and latency targets change. When a primary model is throttled or unreachable, your agents must keep working. They also must act within limits you set and return output other software can use as is. Their answers must stay grounded in sources you allow, and their cost must hold up at high volume. What we shipped in October addresses each of these needs. New models help you match each task to the right price and speed, from high-volume subagents to real-time voice. Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore updates keep agents available, hold them to the processes you define, and help you trust what they return. New pricing and cost reporting make spend more predictable. Strands adds new ways to build, contain, and test agents. Match the model to the task on Amazon Bedrock Run fast, low-cost subagents. Claude Haiku 5.5 is built for subagents and high-volume, cost-sensitive work. According to Anthropic, it is the most capable Haiku yet and costs around 75 percent less than Claude Haiku 4.5 for most tasks. It is also the first Haiku with effort controls, so you can tune cost against intelligence for each task. In a multi-agent setup, a model such as Claude Opus 5.5 can plan the work and hand well-defined coding, tool use, and browser automation tasks to Haiku. This keeps running many agents in parallel affordable. Get near-flagship results at a lower price. OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock. On OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation, it performed on par with GPT-6 Astra and completed tasks more than three times faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Its input and output token prices are at least 50 percent lower than those of GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It accepts text and images with up to 1 million input tokens, which suits drafting proposals, interpreting technical drawings, and building agents that work across business systems. For latency-sensitive work such as real-time coding assistants, GPT-6.1 Sol now also offers Ultrafast mode . Build voice agents that reason in real time. Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic , our latest speech-to-speech model, improves reasoning, instruction following, and tool-calling accuracy, with lower latency at the same price as Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. A customer service agent can now look up an order, check return eligibility, and start a return in a single conversation. Pick specialized models for coding and video. GLM 5.3 by Z.ai is an open-weight model for agentic coding and long-horizon software engineering, with a 1-million-token context window and prompt caching, available to eligible enterprise customers. TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 turns entire videos into structured, time-coded metadata. It reads visuals, audio, and on-screen text in a single pass, with no separate ingestion pipeline. Use more models in AWS GovCloud (US). Claude Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI GPT-5.6 models with cross-Region inference are now available in AWS GovCloud (US). Daybreak Red from OpenAI , a model for authorized security work, is available to eligible customers in AWS GovCloud (US-East). Regulated teams get more models while maintaining US data sovereignty. Build and run agents you can rely on Build and operate agents from your terminal. AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is now generally available in version 1.0 . We rebuilt it with faster startup, a consistent command structure, and support for more AgentCore resources. You can work with harnesses, runtimes, memory, identity, gateways, and payments directly or through a project. Existing projects move to version 1 with one command. The result is one tool from local development to day-to-day operations. Keep agents available when a model is throttled. AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, now supports the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel APIs and model fallback . Your existing Amazon Bedrock SDK code can point at the gateway without per-provider code changes. When the primary model is throttled or unreachable, the gateway routes the request to the next model or provider in a chain you define. A circuit breaker skips destinations that are failing. The gateway can also reach private targets in your virtual private cloud (VPC) using certificates from your own private certificate authority . Your agents stay available without retry logic in every client. Turn your business workflows into agent tools. You can now use AWS Step Functions workflows , including your existing Standard and Express workflows, as tools through AgentCore Gateway. Your business logic stays in a workflow you already run and trust, so you don’t rebuild it inside the agent or rely on a prompt to follow it. The agent decides when to run a workflow, and Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. For example, a support agent can start your refund workflow, and every refund still goes through the same eligibility check, approval, and credit steps. Get JSON your systems can use as is. Structured outputs are now available for all Claude models on Amazon Bedrock. You receive schema-compliant JSON without custom parsing or retries. You can extract every required field from an earnings report, or route support tickets with entities that always match your data model. Keep answers grounded

items.title: Gemini Decisions API
items.description: Gemini Decisions API Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my Yonkers stomping robot video file: dragon: Does this video have a dragon in it? robot: Does this video have a robot in it? france: Is this video set in France? usa: Is this video set in the USA? Jev and OpenAI both return 1.0 or 0.0 for yes/no questions, but Gemini insists on being a little less confident than that: { "dragon" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.04976021841520312 }, "robot" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9234055387792485 }, "france" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.08329171353166241 }, "usa" : { "type" : " yes_no " , "probability" : 0.9230459995157706 } } Via Hacker News Tags: ai , generative-ai , gemini , llm-release , jev , decision-models

items.title: The attendee’s guide to the AWS re:Invent 2026 AI/ML track
items.description: From November 30th to December 4th, Amazon Web Services (AWS) will hold its annual premier learning event: re:Invent . At this event, attendees will become stronger and more proficient in various areas of AWS technology through a variety of experiences: keynotes given by AWS leaders, interactive working sessions led by AWS experts, and fun, immersive activities such as live entertainment and games at re:Play . There are over 2,000 learning sessions that focus on specific topics at various skill levels, and the AI/ML (AIM) track has more than 140 unique sessions for you to choose from. We’re here to help you identify the sessions that best fit your needs. Even if you can’t join in person, you can catch up with many of the sessions on demand and even watch the keynotes live. The basics: Session types If you can join us, then remember that we offer several types of sessions that can help maximize your learning in a variety of AWS topics. re:Invent attendees can choose to attend breakouts, chalk talks, builder sessions, workshops, and code talks. The breakout sessions are recorded and uploaded a few days after to the AWS Events YouTube channel , while the rest are live non-recorded interactive sessions. Here are the details for each session type: Breakout sessions: Attendees are in a lecture-style 60-minute informative session presented by AWS experts, customers, and partners. Chalk-talk sessions: Attendees interact with presenters, asking questions, and using a whiteboard in session. Builder sessions: Attendees participate in a one-hour session and build something. Workshop sessions: Attendees join a two-hour interactive session where you work in a small team to solve a real problem using AWS services. Code talk sessions: Attendees participate in engaging code-focused sessions where an expert leads a live coding session. Lightning talk sessions: Attendees watch a 20-minute demo dedicated to either a specific service or customer story (located in the Venetian Expo Hall or Wynn/Encore Upper Convention Promenade). With so many sessions to pick from, it helps to know how the pieces fit together. Here is how AWS thinks about its AI offerings, so you can decide where to begin and where to focus. The AWS AI stack overview and tie-in to re:Invent sessions AWS offers a comprehensive AI portfolio in the cloud. It covers everything from the physical infrastructure and AI chips that power AI workloads up through ready-to-use agentic solutions that teams can adopt today. Understanding how these services work together helps you navigate re:Invent and focus on the sessions most relevant to what you’re building. Figure 1: The AWS AI stack Global Infrastructure – It all starts with data centers designed and optimized for AI workloads. These facilities are built to handle the power, cooling, and networking demands that large AI training and inference jobs require. AI Chips – Running inside those data centers are two compute options: AWS Trainium , purpose-built for high-performance AI training and inference, and NVIDIA GPUs for teams that need GPU-based acceleration. Customers choose based on their workload, performance requirements, and cost targets. Data Foundation – AI is only as good as the data behind it. AWS Context connects your data across storage, databases, analytics, and search services, giving models and agents access to the right information at the right time. Models, Training, and Inferencing – This is where models get built, trained, fine-tuned, and served. Amazon Bedrock gives you managed access to hundreds of leading models from multiple providers through a unified API. Amazon SageMaker AI gives you full control to train, fine-tune, and deploy custom models on dedicated infrastructure. Many customers use both depending on the workload. Agent Development and Management – Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is where you build, deploy, and manage AI agents. It supports any model or provider mix, including models from both Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker AI, so teams can design agents that pick the right model for each task without being locked into a single provider. Agentic Solutions – At the top of the stack sit purpose-built agents that are ready to use. Kiro helps developers ship correctly the first time with spec-driven development. items.title: Automating AWS Agent Registry updates with push-based architecture
items.description: Every time a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server published in the AWS Agent Registry, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, gains a new tool or updates its schema, the registry record must be updated too. Without automated push-based sync, consumers discover stale metadata. For organizations managing multiple MCP servers across accounts, such a sync keeps catalog records current within an existing governance workflow. In most enterprise deployments, a catalog’s value depends on its freshness. If a developer deploys a new tool on Monday, but the registry record still reflects last week’s schema, consumers lose trust in the catalog. Stale metadata directly reduces registry reliability, leading teams to inadvertently build dependencies on inaccurate information. When an engineer adds a tool to an MCP server but forgets to update the catalog: Consumers miss out on the new capability entirely. Applications might call the tool using an outdated schema, causing unexpected runtime behavior or silent workflow deviations. Multiplied across teams, this lack of automation erodes trust in the registry. Organizations ultimately fall back on ad hoc discovery mechanisms like hardcoded endpoints, informal knowledge sharing, and stale documentation. In this post, we outline an event-driven architecture that automates these updates using AWS CloudTrail, Amazon EventBridge, and AWS Lambda. Architecture overview The following solution brings these services together into an event-driven pipeline that detects runtime changes and synchronizes them to the registry automatically. The architecture supports both multi-account and single-account environments: Single-account setup: For straightforward deployments, all components reside within Account A. Cross-account forwarding setup isn’t needed as events flow directly within Account A. Multi-account setup: This involves two accounts where runtime events from Account B are securely forwarded to Account A. Account A (registry account) owns the AWS Agent Registry, the Amazon EventBridge rule, the push-sync Lambda function, and CloudTrail logs. Account B (MCP server account) hosts the MCP server runtime and the Amazon Cognito OAuth provider used for authentication. The sample uses two accounts, but you can scale the architecture for multiple accounts, with Account A as the registry account and multiple AWS accounts similar to Account B for different MCP servers. The following diagram shows the end-to-end event flow for an update to an MCP server in Account B. The captured event is forwarded to Account A, where a Lambda function queries the MCP server for its tools and updates the matching registry record. Figure 1: End-to-end event flow for a cross-account MCP server update, from the CloudTrail event in Account B to the registry record update in Account A. The architecture uses five AWS services: AWS CloudTrail captures UpdateAgentRuntime API calls as management events. Amazon EventBridge routes matching events to the Lambda function, with cross-account forwarding supported. AWS Lambda queries the MCP server for its current tools, diffs against the registry, and updates the record if changed. AWS Agent Registry stores MCP server records and their tool schemas as the central source of truth. AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, brokers OAuth token exchanges securely, so the Lambda authenticates without storing secrets. How it works: business logic flow After it’s deployed, the pipeline runs the following end-to-end workflow: Trigger : A developer in Account B updates an MCP server, which calls the UpdateAgentRuntime API in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and AWS CloudTrail captures the event. Route : Amazon EventBridge catches the CloudTrail event and forwards it to the central event bus in Account A . Parse : The sync Lambda in Account A extracts the runtime Amazon Resource Name (ARN) from the event payload and dynamically constructs the MCP server’s invocation URL. This is how it knows which server in Account B to query. Authenticate : The Lambda generates a secure OAuth bearer token through AgentCore Identity. Fetch : The Lambda calls the MCP server ( initialize , then tools/list ) to retrieve the latest tools information. Sync : The Lambda finds the matching registry record by its ARN, evaluates the differences, and updates the registry if the schema has changed. This flow assumes that the Agent Registry in Account A already contains a pre-registered record for the MCP server (created during initial onboarding). The Lambda function in this sample updates existing records only. It doesn’t generate new ones. This same flow works in a single-account setup where all resources (registry, Lambda, Amazon EventBridge rule, and MCP server) reside in one account. In that case, skip the cross-account forwarding step. Events flow directly within the same account’s Amazon EventBridge bus. Technical walkthrough This section walks through the workflow for a single MCP server update with two accounts as depicted in the architecture diagram. The same flow executes independently for each server that emits an UpdateAgentRuntime event. The Lambda handles one event at a time, scaling naturally with the Amazon EventBridge invocation model. Step 1: Event capture and routing for cross-account setup When a developer deploys or updates an MCP server, the UpdateAgentRuntime API is called, either by the AgentCore CLI ( agentcore deploy ) or directly. AWS CloudTrail records this as a management event in Account B, with a delivery delay of approximately 5–15 minutes. The event is then delivered to Account A’s default Amazon EventBridge bus. For a cross-account setup, Account B’s Amazon EventBridge forwards matching events to Account A’s event bus through a cross-account rule. The Amazon EventBridge rule target in Account A invokes the sync Lambda, passing the full CloudTrail event JSON as the input payload.
